Bolstered up—The bed. A fitting present—Gloves. Bookkeepers—Book borrowers. A watchword—"What time is it?" Strong reasons make strong actions. A temperate zone—A belt of water. Two heads are better than one—except in the family. You have heard a pin drop, but have you-,heard a cough drop? Flatter a girl by calling her a woman, and a woman by calling her a girl. The way to preserve the peace of a church is to pre- serve the purity of it. To subdue passion and to regulate desire is the great- est task of man as a moral agent. The best way for a smoker to secure peace to his ashes is bv the appointment of a receiver. The man who is 'perpetually hesitating as to which of two things he will do seldom does either. ' What is the difference between a lady and a postage stamp?-0e is a female—the other a mail-fee. One of the hardest things to learn is that the world is seldom watching us when we are doing good. What is the difference between an angler•and a dunce? —One baits his hook; the other hates his book. • We go and fancy that everybody is thinking of us. But he is not; he is like us—thinking of himself. "What tree does the watchdog's honest bark grow upor.. Amelia?" "Upon the bay tree, of course." A girl will naturally express a candid opinion of the young man who is constantly bringing her confectionery. It is the man who determines the dignity of the emu- 1, nation ; not the occupation that measures the dignity/ of the man. Stranger (trying to be friendly) : "How is your healt'Ar Dyspeptic (gruffly) : "How do I know, I haven't, had any for the last five years." With a woman it is a struggle to provide SO mething for the comforts of the inner man, and with n-matt it is an effort to provide something for the outer •emmitti. Small Boy (looking intently at a very bla.ck specimen of the coloured. race): "DA God makelyou, too, cf dust?" C toured Man: "Yes, sonny." Small Boy: "Coal dust?" ar”. Mamma (at the doll counter): "Now, Flossie, dear, here is a very large assortment to select from. What bind of a dolly would you like to have?" Flossie: "Twins, Mamma, if you please." At a school examination the inspector asked a boy why the earth turned round the sun on its own axis. The boy answered with great promptitude, "Because it disna want to get roasted too much on the ane side." " I say," said a smart little son of a country printer who bad just started a local parer, a. he entered a shop in the town, "do you keep knives?" "Oh! yes," res- ponded the shopkeeper "we've kept them for years!" "Well," remarked the boy, starting for the door, "you ought to advertise, and then you wouldn't keep 'ens so long. Mr. Isaacstein: "1 sells you dot coat, my frendt, for say sayventeen toiler; you dake hum along ?" Custo- mer: "I thought. Isaacstein. that ym didn't do busi- ness on Saturday. Isn't this your Sunday?" Mr. Isaacstein (in a low, reverent tone of voice): "My frendt, to sell a coat like dot for sayventeen tollar vas not pees- ness, dot vas charity." Little Bertrand had promised his mother always to count one hundred before speaking after becoming angry. One day his sister snatched an orange from him. and his angry retort came in a suspiciously short time. "Bertrand." said his mother, "did you count one hun- dred?" "Yes'm." "Row did you count it ?' "Ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety, bund'ed." A boy holding a candle to a tradesman allowed tome- thing to attract his attention from the job, so the candle came in contact with the man's head and ignited his hair. After scolding the boy, he made the remark that if the master was to come in. judging by the smell, he would think they had ben singeing a sheep's head. "Wed," replied the boy, "he maybe wadna be fat wiling." Two friends are walking along the street. One of them, pointing to a house, says:—" There's a beautiful place, but it's enough to make a man sad to look at it." "Why so?" "On account of its history, for despite its calm and serene surroundings, it was built upon the groans, tears, wailings, and blood of widows, orphans, old men, and struggling women." " You don't say. Was it built by a railroad monopolist?" "Oh, no; by a dentist." A poet asks—" What are the dreams of the days gone by?" The poet has no business to ask such foolish questions. They are gone, irrevocably gone. You can't put up dreams like you can bottle ketchup or can pre- serves. You have to get all the good you can out of a dream while it is on tap. That's the time to enjoy dreams. Then when the dreams are gone by, if the poet bankers after more, let him eat a mince pie or some pickled tripe before going to bed, and he can secure a new, fresh batch of dreams with no trouble at all.

M. Pasteur will receive after Easter some of his English-speaking admirers who have got up an album which they wish to present to him. It was purchased with the proceeds of a subscription in the United States, Canada, and Great Britain, and opens with the dedicatory inscription to" M. Pasteur, the benefactor of the ;human race,"' ivritten by the Princess of Wales. Her Royal Highness visited the Pasteur Institute when last in Paris.

Dom Pedro and his suite continue to occupy the I whole of the first floor of the Hotel Sejoin, at Nice, greatly to the dismay of the Prince de Joinville and other of his Orleanist relations, who will have to pay the little bill. The Prince deJoinville has done his utmost to persuade Dom Pedro to disafiss some of the members of his numerous suite and to live in more modest style. But this the exiled monarch, who has no notion of the Tally.) of money, and who is a, firm friend, refuses to do. a .

" Count " Dillon, formerly counsellor and treasurer of General Boulanger, is living at present in a hand- some villa at Clarens, on the Lake of Geneva. He has fine horses and carriages, an army of servants, and fares sumptuously every day. His two sons. tall young fellows, are often to be seen with him. I The one is about to enter the Order of the Jesuits. while the other is in a hussar regiment. The " Count" appears to have washed his hands entirely of Boulangism, and turns up his eyes to heaven in a sanctimonious manner whenever the name of the General is mentioned.

There are now placed in the Museum at Pompeii the plaster casts of the bodies of two men and a woman, taken from impressions made in a stratum of aslies outside the Stabian Gate. One of the men had fallen on his baer,and the other,which is remark- ably perfect, on his side, while the woman lies on her face with her arms stretched out. The impression of the tree with foliage and fruit has been examined and found to ,be a variety of the laurus nobilis, the round berries of which ripen in late autumn; and, as the impression found shows the fruit to have been ripe, it seems to prove that the destruction of Pompeii did not occur in August, as believed by many, but in November.

A romantic story is being told of Mrs. Amelie Rives-Chanler, the sometime authoress, who has , adopted the profession of artist. While she was studying in Paris one of her fellow-students, a young fellow of talent, fell in love with her; he made professions of his passion and the fair young lady rebuffed him, but still counted him in her list of good friends. The fellow was by no means dis- couraged. Re continued his importunities, and when Mr. Chanler went to Paris and took his wife on a trip to Algiers the love-sick artist went along, too. It was in Algiers that the unfortunate young man finally recognised the folly and the hopeless- ness of his pursuit. To end his misery, he com- mitted suicide.

It really looks as if the Academicians were going to boycott the Academy Exhibition. Some of the best known men are sending their important work elsewhere. Mr. Long sends his subject picture to the Dore Gallery. Mr. Poynter keeps in the nataloge by a small work. His large picture goes to a dealer's show. Of .Jr. Riviere the samt thing may be said. Mr. Borne Jones has been working hard, but it is into anothergarner than the great storehouse !in Piccadilly that the harvest of his year of ' industry will be gathered. It all seems very strange. Financial reasons may explain it. The dealer gives a big price, and the shillings taken at the doors recoup him part of his purchase money. He has an exhibition of his own,and wants to secure • his attraction. But it is a. question whether he ought to meet with so ready an acquiesc.nce on the part of the painters, and whether the Academicians • do not 9we fealty to their own institution.

Here is a Gull story. which,though a " chestnut" to some, to the thousands who have never heard it is worth telling. Sir William's butler was a great character: a small dark man, always white- chokered, and dressed in black, with a calm solemn manner. His 'income from tips must have been large, as the waiting-room was always crammed, and the order of audience was settled by him. One day, summoned to the street door by a more than ordinary fierce knock, he found an excited indivi- dual just alighted from the cab. "Sir William Gull in?" "Yes, sir." "I want to see him." " Have you an appointment, sir ? " " Appointment ?—no! I'm very ill. I want to see Sir William." "Impos- sible, sir, without an appointment." Naughty word emitted by visitor; then: "When can I see him ?" "Well, sir," after consulting paper, "at eleven on Tuesday next." 'Tuesday next be—! I'm very ill! I tell you I must see some one! Do you know anyone near who could see me ? " Ser- vant, after cogitation: " Well, sir, there's a gentle- man Over the way—a very respectable practitioner named .Tenner—he might be able to see you!"

It was a very steady-going compact little forge, and for some time after its commence- ment employed from fifty to sixty men and boys. When these works had been going on for about ten years the Bewsey works were established by a Com- pany consisting of Messrs. Rylands Bros., Mr. H. Bleckly, and others. These works were established tor the manufacture of wire rods for the purpose of wire-making, and at first employed about fifty men and boys. Mr. Joseph Crosfield began the manufacture of soap, in the year of Waterloo-1815—at Bank Quay, in what had previously been a sugar works.- It iq enough to startle the cleanly housewife of to-day, to learn that at the time Mr. Crosfield founded the works, which are known all over the world-to-day; soap had to bear a tax of no less than .£l4 a ton. Fortunately. however. Mr. Gladstone was instru-r mental, in 1853, in taking off the duty on,soap, and 'since that time. the industry, nationally is well as locally, has progressed, as the phrase is, by leaps and bounds."

One of. the oldest of the multifarious trades carried on in Warrington is that of, glass-making. The first plate glass works in Englsnd Were estab- lished in the year. 1773, at. Ravedhead, near St. Helens, a locality which is still famous for its glass works. Before that dine ' plate glass for use iii England had all to be imported from France. The i i Orford-lane flint glass works were established i Warrington In the year 1797; and -thcntgh at th t time the business was conducted on a very sma I scale, it obtainid pretty lalge diniAgons later 4. and supplied a worldwide detnandi- for the fintr qualities of flint glastz , :‘, •:4 .) t

One of the oldest business; elstlabiis'hMe'artSin Wai- rington is that of the Old Foundry( the presiding Fenius of which is now Mr. James Suiethurst. t is said that this business has a history whi h extends backs to the year 1725. It was founded originally by Mr. Thomas Penketh and remained under the control of the Penketb family until fifteen ago, when it was acquired by Mr. Smethurfit.

Speaking of old local concerns one can hardly luilp mentioninv the firm of Messrs. Greening. A full account of the founder of this firm, as well as of the subsequent history of the house, was given in the " Examiner" a year or two back. It will suffice here to say that this pioneer of the important wiredraw- ing industry of Warrrington,was a young man named Nathaniel Greening. who started business in Bridge- street, in the year 1799. Some years afterwards 'he formed a partnership with the late Mr. John Rylands. the founder of the Rvlands' works, and, indeed, it it a curious fact that nearly all the wire manufacturing establishments of the town have, in one way or another, 'directly or indirectly, origin- ally had some connection with the works set on fhot by the Nathaniel Greening referred to.

The origin of the large and busy establiihment; of the Whitecross Wire and Iron Company was one small wire arawing shop, the whole of the ma- chinery being driven by an engine of thirty horse power. That was close upon thirty years ago, and the whole of the intervening period between now and then has witnessed a rapid yet steady growth of business, and an extension of premises till the company's workshops and storehouses now Over almost as many acres as the original little work- shops did square yards.

Messrs. Robinson, Skinner and Company, Limited, another well-known local firm of flint glass manu- facturers, originatOd about twenty years ago, the promoters being ,Messrs. Peter Robinson, William Robinson and Charles Skinner, the former of whom was at one time in partnership with Mr. Bolton under the style of Robinson and Bolton. The con- cern was, in 1887, converted into a limited liability company.

-- Warrington has long been famous for its ales, and one of the best known manufacturers of this com- modity is the firm of Messrs. Peter Walker and Son. "This celebrated house," we are told, "was founded at Warrington in 1846, by Mr. Peter Walker, who achieved renown in the trade byhis invention of the now widely-used 'Burton Union Casks' for cleansing the beer from yeast." Messrs. Walker have two breweries in Warrington—one in King-st. and the other in Dallam-lane. "The for- mer was the original location of the business, and here Mr. Peter Walker, after 'considerable expe- rience as a brewer in Ayr, started the prosperous career of the influential house that bears his name." Owing to the increase of business, the Dallam-lane brewery was built in 1865. It is said that the weekly output of this firm's Warrington breweries is upwards of 7,500 barrels, to say nothing of the liquor they brew at their Burton establishment. Sir A. B. Walker is now the sole proprietor of this great business, although his two sons, Mr. W. H. Walker and Mr. J. R. Walker, are actively engaged in it, the former superintending the operations at Warrington, and the latter at Burton-on-Trent.

and Cage Birds," with coloured plates. These works are being issued in parts, price 6d. each. "We have also to hand the current issues of •" Cassell's Family Magazine," "The Quiver," "Little Folks;" "The Dore Gallery '." "Illustrated Shakespeare ;" "The Sea ;" " The World of Adventure ." "The Story of the Heavens ;" and " Familiar Wild Flowers." In the " English Men of Letters" series, edited by Mr. John Morley, and published by Messrs. Macmillan and Co., we! have the volume on the poet Keats, from the pen of Mr. Sidney Colvin. Keats will ever hold his place in the front rank of English poete and eVerythillg relating to him is therefore of deep Interest. This bin. raphy has been prepared after careful mai patient re- search ;it contains much new matter and settles some disputed points. It is written in a Critical, and yet ia a sympathetic spirit, and causes the reader to feel that he can justly admire Keats, both sea poet and as a man. "By the World Forgot" is the title of a one-volume shilling novel, published by Messrs. F. Warne and Co. It is written by Mr. E. J. Clayden, and it is out of the common run of books of this class. It is pleasantly written, healthy in tone, and the thread of the story is well kept in hand from beginning to end. "Now and Then," or, "Through a Glass Darkly" i (6d.), is also issued by Messrs. Warne and Co. It s sufficient to ensure it a large body of readers to say that it is from the pen of Mr. Samuel Warren, F.R.S., the celebrated author of "Ten Thousand a Year," and "The Diary of a late Physician." "The Three Midshipmen," by the late W. H. Kingston, is issued by Messrs. Griffith, Ferran, and Co., as a 6i. volume. It is pleasantly written, full of adventure, and makes capital reading, especially for boys. From Mr. Elliott Stock, London, we have to hand "The Antiquary" for March, with papers, amongst others, on " Holy Wells," "Old Bradford," "At the Grosvenor Gallery," "Wilmington Grant," &c. We have also part 3, price 6d., of "Handbook of Literary, Scientific, and Bible phrases " ; and part 3of the "Field Club, a magazine of natural history for scientific and unscientific readers," price 3d. The" Ladies Gazette of Fashion" for March contains

two coloured fashion plates, and numerous other illustra- tions 4 the spring fashions, with articles on " Society and Pashio-n," " Plaking the Violin," "Round the Shop," '6 Decorations in Hampton Court," " New Coiffures," "March in the Garden," kc. "The Ladies' Treasury" for March is beght and varied as usual. It is always a good sixpenny worth of" litera- ture, education, and fashion."

In. %tore/Mak wishes to see you, sir." Mark Woolford looked up had:ly from his Writing table, and nodded to the clerk. ..rn go directly," he replied; and as soon as the man had left his room he began to walk up and down hastily, for the summons meant trouble. " Rothing like facing troubles," be said with a bitter smile, and, checking a sigh, he went straight to the managerial sanotum. "Where's Martin?" said the old man, sharply, for Mr. IClopstock at Tlumphreys' was a very different individual to Mr. lilopetock visiting in Brunswick- square. "I don't know—l expected to find him here," said Mark, anxiously. "Nothing fresh, I hope." " Didn't you see him last night ? " said the old man, evasively, as he snapped first his snuff-box and then hit fingers. "Then he is off somewhere on the loose," said old Klopstook, with a heavy frown settling upon his face. "Now, look here, Woolford business is business, is it not?"

"Undoubtedly." "Very well then: we lead two liven. Away from here we know one another, and visit and play rubbers at whist, and talk politics. I Euppose we are friends." 'I hope so, I'm sure—nay, I know we are," said Mark, smiling. "Don't grin," said the old man, sharply. "It's no laughing matter. Listen to me." Mark bowed, and took a seat. He knew the old man too well to feel offended. "Here at the office you are chief clerk, and I am manager; and, to speak plainly, you do your work very well, and I don't dislike you quite so much as I do the other clerks." Mark bowed again, and suppressed the smile, for he saw that the worthy old fellow was greely put out. "Now, just understand me,Woolford," he continued, "I won't have home life and office life mixed up. Humphreys give me full charge here. They never interfere; in fact, I feel sometimes as if I do just as I please with them instead of they with me. So look here. As I say, rn not have friendship and business mixed. If you don't do your duty I shall supersede even you—l tell you to your face; and, what's more, if I felt that I didn't do my bit of management right by Humphreys and Company, rd throw up my place to-morrow. What do you say to that?" "I feel sure you would," said Mark, warmly. "Very well then, Woolford, can you expect a man who would not spare himself, nor yet the very best chief clerk in the City of London, to put up with the confounded, insolent, jackanapisb, puppyish im- pertinence of a careless, insignificant, worthless, use- less boy who sets a bad example to all the other clerks in the place, and whom I could supersede to the silvan. tage of the firm with a boy fresh from school?" " It is very, very hard," said Mark, sadly. "Hard! Demme, sir, hard isn't the word. Adamant's pap and diamonds are soft cheese to it. Hard! There, I tell you that in the whole course of my career, as a commercial man, I never had to deal with such a reckless young stamp. There, there, there, hear me out. One of us in a passion is quite enough at a time. I don't mind his insolence and gibes when I come to see you. He shows off so as to serve me out, as he thinks, poor fool! But I don't mind it, not a bit, and he may say and do whatever he pleases outside these walls; but he's paid so much money every month to do so much work for Hum- phreys and Company, and hang it, Woolford., I will have it done. There's nothing wrong in that, ie there?" "No. no; of court* not, but—" , "Now look here, Woolford, I've not done. Hear me out, please. What I want to say is this: Your brother is young and too fast, and I've stood it as long as lean. If be don't regulate those books of his or get them put right, I shall be obliged—this is final, mind—l say I shall be obliged, out of a stern feeling of duty to Humphreys and Company, to call upon him to resign." "To resign!" said Mark, sadly. "Resign. Yes, of course. Why, if it was Roby, or Juker, or Layeoek, or Brown, sir, I should give him his salary down on the desk,•and tell the porter to open the door and see him off the premises. • I Shall call upon him—and I've no business to do it—to reeign. ' "No, no, Klopstoek---" "Mr. Klopstock, if you please," said the old man, sharply. "I beg your pardon, Mr. Klopstock, my dear old friend," said Matk, earnestly. "I'm not your old friend here, sir," cried the manager, with asperity. "Thus is Humphrey and Company's place of business, and we are paid servants of the Arm." "Yes, yes, of course; but I beg, Mr. Klopstock, that you will not proceed to extremities at present," cried Mark, earnestly. "Why not? He's a nuisance to me from his im- pertinent neglect, and a constant source of worry to you. He presumes uon your being chief clerk to take the most unwarrantable liberties. I've seen it plainly enough these two years past, The erm would be better served, and your =Veit here would be ten tine .• as comfortable withosiZ him." " And about my position at home when he was away ? " said Mark, drily. "That's nothing to do-with the firm, sir," said the Did man, sharply. "I say you would be ten times as eomfortable here without him." "Never mind that," cried Mark, earnestly. "Look ; here—l MR speaking the honest truth—Martin is getting on the right track now. There are reasons for It. We are winning him over to a better way, and, in a short time, I'm sure all will be right. A man cannot 'flange in a day." "Can't he! But he must. He shall change, and in half a day, or half an hour, or he shan't stop here. I shall have all the other clerks laughing at me directly, end setting meat defiance." " Have a little more patience," said Mark, Imploringly, " rio sure this will bring him round." " What, little Ruth ?" Mark winced, but bowed his head. "Never. He hasn't it in him, and you're doing wrong by the pretty little lassie by encouraging it. Better by far marry her yourself." ,"Mr. Klopstock !" Ah, I mean it. She's a good girl, awl if I were forty years younger, I should like to marry hermyself. I say you—are—do—ing—wrong—by en—cou—rag— ing—it," he cried, giving the table a rap with the corner of his snuff-box between every syllable. "No, no—nonsense. They love each other," said Mark, hastily. "More fool she !" grumbled the old man. "Come, you'll look over it this time," said Mark. "I feel sure that this will bring him round." "Not it," said the old wan. viciously, taking another pinch of snuff. "That boy will never make a man of business. I know better." , "Come, come," exclaimed Mark, smiling; "don't be prejudiced." Woolford!" exclaimed the old man, severely, "I ask you, as chief clerit in this old-established firm, whether that is a proper way to address the manager? Prejudiced, insleed! Lac* here, on': Out of offict• hours, sir, you may call me a Prejudiced old fool it , yod like, but in °face hours —, there, sir," he cried. fuming, "if such • thing occurs again, I'll send in a report to the partners in the firm." "My dear Klepstock, I beg Your pardon—l do, indeed, my dear old friend,'; said Mark, who thoroughly understood the old man's ways. "But now; about Martin." "Well, what about him!'" said the old man, win: was somewhat mollified. "You will not ask him to resign ?" "Well, if you beg me nor, I suppose I must no this time; but you take notice of my words—l say w- bad better send him away, or we shall both live te bitterly regret it. There's no hiding the fact, Mark,' said the old man, in a low, pained tone of voice "the boy is not honest," Mark's head went down upon his hand. "And be is the son of a woman who—God bles, her—was as near an approach to an angel as woman could be. Mark, I loved your poor mother very dear] when I was young." "Yes," said Mark, gently, as he took' the hand extended to him, and pressed it warmly, "I always believed you did." " I did, my boy, dearly," continued the old man, forgetting business now; "but when I saw that 5,,- loved another, and a better man, I told myself tlict her happiness was my great aim, and I never let her know I was anything but a very good friend." "To my father and my mother," said Mark.

warmly. "Well, well, well," said the old fellow. "I tried to be, Mark, I tried to be, and—hang it, sir, what are we talking about? This is not business." The old fellow seemed quite transformed once more. "No," said Mark, smiling, "friendship crept in for a moment." "Yes. and it won't do. Now. look here. Mark. I

say we shall both of us regret what we have dune eh?—that is if Ido consent to it. I anybody con till me, that lam belog euc of a grest act of weakness, and I prophecy that the will come when you and I will bitterly repenr. AIM feel now foolish we have been." : No,. no," said Mark, warmly, wringing his hand. "Don't talk like that. Look here. Mr. -Klopstock. The lad is high spirited, and perhaps a liule weak but tve is toning down. I muds—l will ee him settleatatwn into a gOkia member of society. He is my brothir, and ate 'harp rests upon me of helping Mai onward Klopstock, old friend, we must leave business for moment whist I say to you, I know you would sooner lend me your aid in this work than go against me." " Well, yes, I suppose I would," said the old man, quietly, as he took a fresh pinch of snuff, and then snapped tile box, as if he were trying to bite something with it. "It's a great nuisance, though, this being obliged to help and pet peopla you do not like. He is . your brother, Mark, but at the sometime he is about as great an eyesore to me as there is in the place." "Yes, I know he worries you, but you will help use to bring him round?" "Well, well, look here—shall I have him in, and give him a good sound talking to when he comes Y added the old man. "No, no; no, no," exclaimed Mark, hurriedly, " V would—" "Make him kick over the traces. Yea, of course. I have not got a very amiable way with me," said the old man, grimly. "There, then, have it your own way. But mind this, Mark Woolford, our duty tic the firm should make us take especial note of the sets of this young gentleman. We know rather too much ae it is. "Of his past, let us say," said Mark, umilir,g. "Cl the present and fusure let us hope for better things." "Yes; but he's fast—very fast," said the old man. " Was fast—say was," replied Mark, smiling. "Shan't!" exclaimed the old manager. "1 say he is fast, and there are great temptations to a young man in a place like this. Hadn't we better get rid of him while our shoes are good?" "For heaven's sake, don't talk like that." exclaimed Mark, flushing. "Why not?" said Klopitock, grimly; "a man wht, gambles is never safe." Well, but, I gamble," exclaimed Mark—" largely." "You? Bah I Stuff !.Tell one the world is standing on its bead in a soup plate, sir, and l'll just as G 0312 believe you." " But I do in docks and snares." " Ah-h-h!" exclaimed the old men. "Well, if that's gambling I'm in the swim too. I say, Mark, Benares bonds are going down every day. They must rise soon, understand. ti.srb sop. word to the wise. Now be ofL I've half a dozen letcers to write, and I'm sure you have enough to do." "Quite," said Mark, smiling. " K.lopstock, I shall never forget this;" and he left the room. "I hope we shall neither of us have cause tic remember it, Mark, my boy," said the old man, soi ; "but I can't feel that we are doing right, had I shall never feel safe while that fellow, Martin, is about the place. Ugh! the thought of it makes me shudder." Meanwhile, Mark Wool 'ord had gone hack to his own room, with the smile dying off his lips as coon as he was alone, for his spirit was very sad within him, and be could not help wondering how it would alt cad. div.p: NEW BOOKS, &c.

"Choice Cookery," by Miss H. M. Young, of War- rington, has reached a second edition. It is published by Mr. John Heywood, of Manchester, at the price of two shillings, and is so admirably pre- pared that it is likely to be in demand for a long time to come. It is intended as" a practical guide to those ladies desirous of becoming acquainted with the art of cooking in its choicest and most economical form." As the recipes have for the most part been given at the public demonstrations on cooking by the authoress, ix is a matter of course to say that they will be found thoroughly reliable. • "Domestic Cookery, with special reference to cooking by gas," by the same practical writer, is issued by the same publisher, and at the same price as " Choice Cookery." It may be taken as evidence of its great popularity that it has reached the Bth edition. The work was issued originally to meet the requirements of the ladies who had attended the lectures on Cookery, and the object, it need hardly be said, is to give the inform- ation in a plain and practical form. Miss Young believes in using the gas steve,when convenient, and her instruc- tions on the gas rangia will be especially beneficial to those who are at liberty to apply such apparatus. Cookery is an art not sufficiently studied in this country, and there is, therefore, a good deal of waste and not a little indigestion. It would pay most housewives many times over to purchase one or both of the two volumes under notice. Mr. Heywood also publishes a capital" Lodal examin- ation history from before the Roman invasion to the present time." It is issued for the use of students pre- paring for the local examinations, in connection with the Universities of Oxford ard Cambridge' and the Royal College of Preceptors. The writer, Dr. R. S. Pringle, is a practical teacher who has been so successful that not one of his candidates has ever failed in the history paper. This valuable work has been revised and extended, and has reached the 11th edition. Another useful work for students reaches us with the title of " Delecourt's French Instructor." It is published as a practical method of acquiring a useful knowledge of the French tongue. It contains models of composi- tion by the best authors, with exercises, notes, vocabu- lary, and a complete system of French commercial cor- respondence. As far as we can judge from a cursory examination, it seems admirably arranged with a view to meeting the wants of French students. It is pub- lished by Mr. Heywood ; price 2s. Cassell's "Magazine of Art" for March has for frontispiece a beautiful photogravure of "Saved," from a picture by Frank Bramley. Mr. E. F. Brewtnall, R.W.S., formerly of Warrington, contributes a charm- ing paper on" Winter in the country," which he has most admirably illustrated. Amongst other noteworthy illustrated articles may be mentinned "Old Masters and deceased British artists ; " " Art patrons," " The Im- perial Instituto ;" and " M. L. Solon." In "The Women's World" we have "Lady Sandhurst at Home," with a portrait of her Ladyship; Women as Disunionists" ; "The leaders of the Imperial Seraglio"; "Tudor Exhibition," illustrated; "Modern Jewellery.," and the usual review of illustrations of current fashions. The "Cabinet Portrait Gallery" for March contains beautifully finished portraits (with accompanying sketch) of Mr. Frank Lockwood, Q.C., M.P., "The Duchess of Leinster," and "Signor Piatti." We cannot too highly praise these artistic photographs, and it is no more than due to say that the biographical sketches are written with brightness and discrimination. Amongst the new publications issued by Messrs. Cassell and Co., are "The World of Wonders," being an illustrated record of things wonderful in nature, science, and art ; and an "Illustrated Book on Canaries
ALLEGED SUNDAY DRINKING AT WARRINGTON.

On Monday, at the Warrington Police Court, George Brooks, beerhouse keeper, Wilderspool-road was summoned for having kept his premises open during prohibited hours on the 16th March.—Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins appeared for the defendant.— _ __

Inspector Spinks said that at 10.55 a.m. on the Sun- day in question he went into Wilderspool-road. He saw a number of Ship Canal labourers loitering near the Crossing. From what he observed he, in Com- pany with Constables Monaghan and Rowbottom, suddenly turned up the opening leading to the side door of defendant's house. When within ayard or two of the door he saw a man come out, and the door was closed behind him. The man, who was drunk, was stopped, and gave his name and address as John Brown, 6, Rose- and-Crown-St. Witness tapped gently at the door; it was opened by the defendant, and the officers entered, taking with them the man Brown. In the tap-room there were two tables. On the first table there were four pint jugs, three containing beer and one porter. On the opposite table were a large jug and a spirit glass, with which the occupants of the room, ten in all, were serving the beer out to one another. The men were all, more or less under the influence of drink. Witness said to the landlord "How do you account for this, on a Sunday morning, when p,ople are going to church ? " Defendant hesitated a moment, and then said " Eight of them are lodgers and two are bona fide travellers." Witness took the names and addresses of the men, and it turned out only two were lodgers. Brown had been summoned. In reply to Mr. Jenkins, witness said that defendant did not say that eight were bona fide travellers, and two were lodgers. Two of the men said they hail come from the Big Field. Runcorn. There was no bread or cheese about. The landlord said that Brown had not been in the house until he came in with the constables. He said that Brown had been in the yard, which could be reached without going through the house. It was untrue that the police officers were concealed in some willows.—P.O. Monaghan and 'P.C. Rowbotton corroborated.—Mr. Jenkins, addressing the Bench for the defence, said that his client, although he had kept- a licensed house for 16 years. had never had any charge or complaint made against him before. He contended that Brooks had not committed a breach of the law, and that if the magis- trates had any doubt about the case they should give his client the benefit of it. He then called Henry Caxton, a Ship Canal navvy, who said that he lodged at the house of the defendant. He remembered Sundly, the 16th. Between 10 and 11 o'clock he was in the kitchen, wash- ing himself. Through the window he saw Brown come from the road up the passage. He appeared to be tipsy .at the time, and afterwards went into the yard at the back. The police afterwards took Browninto the house, and questioned him. There were eight lodgers and two travellers in the house. The latter had some bread and cheese, but, as far as he knew, they had no beer.— I Defendant,called, said he was the landlord of the house in question. On the previous night to Sunday the 16th inst., eight men lodged at his house. Two other men called at the house in the morning, and stated that they had travelled from Runcorn, and were on their way to Salford. He questioned them, as was usual, and was satisfied that they were travellers. With respect to Brown, witness said that he had not been in his house, neither had he supplied him with any drink that morn- ing. Brown himself denied having been in the house. -- The magistrates then retired for consultation with their Clerk, and on their re-appearance the Mayor said that the magistrates were of opinion that there was doubt in the case, and although they thought the police officers had done their duty, they were inclined to give the defendant the benefit of the doubt and dismiss the case.
WELSH CONCERT AT WARRINGTON.

On Monday evening a concert was held in tlie Sankev-st. Co-operative Hall in aid of the proposed ne* Welsh Church for Warrington. The Mayor (Alderman Francortib) presided, and there was a large attendance, the hall being filled. From a musical point of view the annual Welsh concert is always a success, and there\ was no deterioration in this respect on Monday evening. The artistes were —soprano, Miss Jennie Jones; contralto, Miss Annie Parry; tenor, Mr. J. T. Jones; bass, Mr. Fred Owens; humorist, Mr. Llew. Wynne; solo harp, Miss Toft; solo carnet, Mr. R. Bennett. • solo piano- ; accompanist, G. Rile 3 Allrer piano- forte, success, Ms er . t a 1 Davies; rn acquitted themselves with co- , end the recalls were pretty frequenit I p In the first part of the programme Miss Jennie Jones was encored for her rendering of "A Song from Heaven," and Mr. Fred Owens was similarly honoured for "The Bedouin Love Song." Miss Mit, was loudly applauded for her-harp solo. 'Bells .of Aberdovey" and had to bow her acknowledg- ments, while Mr. Wynne, who is a really amusing humorist, had to reappear after his humorous sketch" A rural railroad ride." Mr. Richard Ben- nett and Miss Annie Parry also deservedly secured much applause. Mr. George Riley, it is needless to say, made a most accomplished accompanist. Dur- ingthe interval

l'he MAYOR said that while thinking over what he might say at that meeting he had been struck with the fAct that during the whole of the time he had spent at the bridewell as a magistrate he never once met with a Welshman. (Hear, hear.) He was the more struck with this fact when he was told that there was a considerable number of Welsh people in the town, because they generally found that when a number of people of a particular nationality were in a neighbourhood ' there were some black sheep amongst them. He found that there were about 100 Welshmen on the Ship Canal, and also that they had a good congregation of Welsh people worshipping in Bold-st. That congregation was deserving lof the help of the people of Warrington, and he trusted that before long they would have a church worthy of their own earnestness, and that whenever they were visited by friends from the ancient mountains, their native land, they would be able to say that the church had been built by their own industry and by the help of the people of Warrington. (Applause.) The ttev. J. R. Everts, having mentioned that the special object of that gathering was to raise funds for the building of a Welsh Church, said that he wished it to be understood that the Welsh Church in Warrington did not mean to establish itself at the expense of any other church in the town. There was a large number of Welsh people who came to that town who could not, owing to their deficiency in the English language,join in the services of any English Church,and if it were aot for the Welsh Church in all probability many of these people would be lost to all religious teaching. Twelve months ago the Welsh Church in Bold-st. had only 46 members, but now, notwithstanding that there had been 15 or 20 removals, the membership was close upon 80. (Ap- plause.) Last Sunday he preached on the Ship Canal,and they were about fifty persons present at the service. Re was assurred that there were about 100 Weishinen work- ing on that one section of the canal, and no doubt, as the wont got nearer to the town, there would be still more. There were also about 50 Welsh young women in service in and around Warrington, and nearly all of them attended the Welsh Church in Bold-st. With regard to the proposed new church, Mr. Evans mentioned that last year they had between £BO and £lOO promised, but now tiey had about £lOO in hard cash in ,hand, and about another £5O in promises. They were, therefore, getting nearer, but they did not feel , justified in beginning to build till between £2OO and £3OO was in hand. • (Hear, hear.) He then moved a vote of thanks to the Mayor, to Miss Tat, Mr. Bennett, and Mr. Riley, andthis having been seconded, was cordially passed.

sleep was. poor; he tumbled around on his bed the
most of the night, and had such frightfo'
dreams he was afraid to sleep, .much as he
needed the sweet restorer. There was a nauseous taste

in his mouth, and his food sat on his stomach like a dead, heavy load. Then be grew moody, nervous, and irri- table,and could hardly give a civil answer to a question. He felt as though some evil was going to happen in his

family or in his affairs, although what it could be he couldn't imagine. One evening, on getting up Suddenly from his chair to respond to a call, he was taken. with a giddy, whirling sensation, and almost fell to the floor. Thoroughly alarmed he sent for a physician, and. in the coarse of the illness which followed, be was attended by the best medical men from various large cities; and, to
use Mr. Ellis' own words "they doctored 'and blistered till there was very little of me left." His bowels were
costive, skin dry and tot, eyes yellow, hands and feet cold and clammy. For months he existed on nothing
but a little tea or coffee and bread daily. Even on this
simple diet the agony he endured after eating was some-
thing he Gould not find words for.

At last he was about to give up in despair, when his wife, a retiring, quiet woman, said, "My dear husband, there is one thing I believe would help you—Mother Seigel's Syrup." She had used it, but he had not. ' " Stuff and humbug !" he answered testily; "when the doctors fail, I see no reason to pin my faith to a patent medicine. Elit you may be right ; anyhow, I'll do it to oblige you. It can't make me any worse."

So she procured a bottle, and in twenty-four hours he felt the welcome relief. In three days he was able to take a little meat, and before he had finished the second bottle, he enjoyed hisdneals regularly. This is now three years ago, and he is still in the best of good health, and when last we heard from him le was planning a visit to his old home in Ireland.
In his last letter to a frieird, Mr. Ellis says: "Speaking of my recovery, I want to say I am sure I should now be underground if I hadn't taken my wife's advice, and used Mother Seigel's Syrup."

div.head: STABBED TO DEATH.
div.p: STABBED TO DEATH.

At the inquest held on Tuesday, at Ashby-de:la-Zouch, relative to the death of Samuel Haywood, sanitary pipe •manufacturer, who was stabbed on Monday, a verdict pf wilful murder was returned against his assailant, Richard Nicklinson. The latter was in the service of Haywood, his brother:in-law, and had, it is stated, neglected work. A guar* arose and the two men fought, Nicklinson afterwards dbgging Haywood and stabbing I him to death. The prisoner was brought before the ' magistrates on Tuesda* and stated that he had only acted in self-defence.

div.head: ELECTION INTELLIGENCE
div.p: ELECTION INTELLIGENCE

EAST DOWN. The nomination of candidates for the vacancy in the Parliamentary representation of East Down, caused by r the resignation of Captain Kerr, Conservative, took place at Downpatrick on Tuesday. Dr. J. A. Rantoul, Liberal Unionist, was the only candidate nominated, and he was accordingly declared duly elected.

WINDSOR. Mr. Gladstone has written a letter to the Liberal can- didate for Windsor expressing satisfaction that he should have come forward to take his share in "fighting the battle." The right honourable gentleman trusts that Mr. Grenfell will make the best use of the vacancy, because " the Government feel that they are floating ' down upon Niagara." The Mayor of Windsor, Mr. J. L. Hollis, late on Wed- nesday night received the writ for the election of a mem- ber of Parliament to succeed Mr. Richardson Gardner, Conservative, resigned. He has fixed the nomination for Monday next, and the polling for the following Vi'edneeday.

ASHTON-UNDER-LYNE. At a meeting of the Liberal executive at Ashton-under- Lyne, on Saturday night, it was announced that Mr. Herbert Rhodes, cotton spinner, of Glossop, had accepted an invitation to become the .Gladstouian candidate for the borough at the next election. CARNARVON. Mr. Lloyd George, the Gladstonian Liberal candidate for Carnarvon Borough, issued his address on Monday. He favours Home Rule for Ireland, Disestablishment of the Welsh Church, and a wider form of self-government for Wales. Mr. Issard Davies has declined to stand in the Conservative interest. It is now proposed to ask Mr. Marehant Williams, barrister, of London, to accept the • candidature. AYR BURGHS ELECTION. A UNIONIST VICTORY.

Polling commenced on Tuesday morning for the elec- tion of a member of Parliament for the Ayr Burghs in room of Mr. John Sinclair, Gladstonian Liberal, resigned. The candidates were Mr. Edmund Routledge, Gladston- ian Liberal, and James Somerville, Conservative. Voters appeared both at Irvine and Ayr in considerable num- bers, and the greatest interest appeared to be taken in the election. °Vehicles were largely used. Both candi- dates visited the town, and were heartily received. ' Great excitement prevailed at Ayr, and scarcely any business was done. The result of the polling in the Ayr Burgs was declared O 1 Wednesday as under : Mr. J. Somerville (Unionist) Mr. E. Routledge (Liberal)

Majority The declaration by Sheriff Baird caused great excite- ment, and there was an immediate rush to the telegraph Office and to the committee-rooms. Mr. Somerville at- tempted to address his supporters, but could not get himself heard. The new member then entered a carri- age, which was drawn by the crowd to Newton, where he briefly addressed the people. He said the result _l4:owed that the working men of Ayr could still be trusted. Mr. Routledge also addressed a large gathering' of his suroPorters. He said they bad been beaten at the poll, but were not disheartened. The victory would not, he . .
- thouYht, do the Tory party much good. (Cheers.)

• TRIAL OF CHADWICK FOR THE ATHERTON MURDER.

At the Liverpool Assizes on Monday, before Mr. Justice tdathew, William Chadwick, aged twenty-eight, des- nribed as a labourer, was indicted for having at Ather- ton, on the 22nd July last, murdered a pawnbroker's assistant named Walter Davies, who formerly lived at Vidnes.

Mr. Watson, who opened the prosecution, stated that thC case very largely depended on what was called cir- cumstantial evidence. On the morning of the murder the deceased received instructions from his employer tm swill out the cellar and dress the window in the ordinary fashion. Mrs. Clewes, one of the witnesses for the pro- secution, saw deceased dressing the window after eight o'clock. Afterwards she had occasion to visit the shop, but after repeatedly calling deceased obtained no answer. She again returned to the shop, and once more failing to elicit a reply went for her son, and on returning they found deceased lying in the cellar in the midst of several Pools of blood. Life'was not then quite extinct, but After a gasp or two he expired, and the medical evidence *lowed that deceased had a number of punctured 'wounds and bruises about the head, the most important one being a punctured wound an inch below the right ear, cutting through the lobe. Several witnesses gave evidence as to prisoner being. Seen in the vicinity of the shop on the morning of the ilee, and a Manchester pawnbroker identified him as -aving pledged one of the watches at his establishment. The case was not concluded at the rising of the Court.
TIE CORPODATION BILL.
ANOTHER TOW.N'S MEETING.-LIVELY
PROCEEDINGS.

On Monday evening another meeting of Warring- ton ratepayers, convened by the Mayor, was held in the Public Hall, for further consideration of " The Warrington Extension,Water,and I mprovement Bill." The meeting was of an informal character, and had been called by the Mayor in compliance with the wishes of several influential ratepayers. The Mayor (Alderman Francomb) presided in the early part of the meeting, and afterwards the Deputy-Mayor (Alderman Sutton) took the chair. There were also on the platform Alderman Harrison; Councillors W. Pierpoint, F. Monks, J. H. Fleming, E. Greenall, W. H. J. Jenkins, R. T. Fairclough, J. Fairclough ; Messrs. T. Morris, T. Birchen. John Walker, J. L. Tunstall, T. Tunstall,W..Diggle, Spinks,Taylor ; J. L. Whittle (Town Clerk), and T. Longdin (Borough Surveyor). There was not a large attendance of ratepayers. .. - -

The MIYon said: This is an informal meeting called for the purpose of giving any of the rate- payers an opportunity of further discussing the meritsof the bill. I propose to lay a statement before you showing what part the Corporation have taken since the last meeting, and in order, if pos- sible, to lay the facts clearly before you.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

On Tuesday the trial ;as The court was again crowded, and Chadwick was again accommodated With a seat in the dock. Evidence for the prosecution was proceeded with, as 'Nieves :—Daniel Perry, manag,er for his mother, a pawn- broker of Brownlow-hill, Liverpool, said on the day of the muraer a gold watch was pledged for £6 by a man Whom he could not identify. They had a special con- tract book in which to enter such transactions. The contract was signed bi the pledger in the name of " Fred Smith, 113, Lime-street, Liverpool." He pro• duce d that signature. t„ James Berry, saddler, living at Eccles, said he h ad_ 'ccm'n Chadwick since June. He had only stammered , ! that St times. On one occasion when he was in witness's shop he remarked that his hair was ' different colour to his moustache, and asked if he could not have something to make the latter the same eolour as his hair. On the subsequent day witness gave • some hair dye, and the witness that time wanted to 'ail him some brushes. When he was getting them out the bag witness observed him put a piece of cosmetic :in his waistcoat pocket. t„Some stir was caused in court when the name of John ; 'r-ciward Lorne was called. He did not answer, and the , rdence of Sergeant Chipchase was taken, at the coa- :,tinsion of which the Court was adjourned. ‘• WEDNESDAY.—VERDICT AND SENTENCE. 0n Wednesday the prisoner's wife, who was in court troitg,hout the previous day, again occupied a seat close the dock, separated only about a couple of yards from be husband. It was understood on Tuesday night that he C 55 for the prosecution had closed, but on Wednes- "ar morning Mr. Watson recalled Superintendent Weir' who spoke of railway conveni- . v_vces at Atherton, the town being, he said, 12 or 13 'ices from Manchester. There were several stations, and trains were very frequent on both lines of railway. THE JUDGE SUMMING UP. Bit Lordship .then summed up the case to the jury. Dealing with the evidence, his Lordship said e ere was not the slightest evidence that anyone had trhkertained any enmity against the deceased. As to the t Z°cY that someone may have gone into the shop and the watches and not have been the murderer, he ought that was obliterated by the fact that the murdered e•-'au's watch and chain were taken. div.head: a&A.yon's STATEMENT.
div.p: THE a&A.yon's STATEMENT.

In speaking, at the request of the Council, to solicit your support of thq Corporation in their de- cision to extend the Borough Boundary, purchase the Water Works, and carry out other improvements, I will first state that all matters of difference which caused an adverse vote at the Meeting of Ratepayers have been satisfactorily 'adjusted.

div.head: EXTENSION OF THE BonougH.
div.p: EXTENSION OF THE BonougH.

No objection was raised against, in fact there was unanimity in favour of, the extension of the Borough Boundary, which the Corporation believe will be distinctly an advantage, not only to the existing Borough, but also to the parts proposed ts be added.

div.head: PITRCHASE OF THE WATER WORKS.
div.p: PITRCHASE OF THE WATER WORKS.

The subject of the purchase of the Water Works undertaking seems to be the bone of contention in the Bill, and some of the objectors to the purchase seem to have misconceived the object the Corpora- tion have in view by the clauses in the Bill. It was at first proposed to apply to Parliament for powers to enable the Corporation to purchase the works corepulsorily, but afterwards deemed desirable that before such application was made every effort should be made to purchase the undertaking up- on terms to be mutually agreed upon ; and with this view a deputation was appointed by the Corporation to wait upon the Water Works Com- pany. The directors were advised by their Parlia- mentary Counsel that in order to maintain their legal position in the event of our proceeding for compulsory purchase they must refuse to negotiate with the Corporation so long as such clauses remained part of the Bill. The compulsory clauses have therefore been abandoned, and the object now sought is simply to enable the Corporation to pur- chase upon such terms as may be mutually agreed upon, and to obtain the transfer to tl.e Corporation of the powers of the Company under their private Acts of Parliament. I may point out that the Cor- poration have already power under the Public Health Act to purchase the Water Works undertak- ing without the Bill, and,if I 'hay reiterate,the Bill if approved by the poll will only transfer to the Corporation the statutory powers of the Company in the event of the terms of purchase being here- after mutually agreed upon. The Corporation are in no way pledged to the offer of 30 years' purchase,and the overtures made to the Company are conditional upon a proper examination of the Company's pro- perty and accounts. It is possible that the Corporation may for some reason find it undesirable to purchase, or the terms may be altered upon further negotiations with the Company; but it must not be lost sight of that the acquisition of the Water Works undertaking upon fair terms, and by this I mean terms which will not be a burden to the ratepayers,is ot vital importance to the town and the inhabitants. The Corporation believe that the time has arrived when the purchase on such terms should be effected. It is also believed that if the purchase is further delayed, the Com- pany will require a much larger amount than the sum which has been named as the purchase price of their undertaking. Most of you will have seen the report prepared by Mr. J. L. Tunstall, in which he deals with the two methods of establishing the necessary Sinking Fund for the repayment of the purchase money, and it may not be out of place shortly to explain the two methods in which the Sinking Fund may be established by law. Suppos- ing 60 years were allowed by Parliament for the repayment of the money, the Corporation will have the option of repaying the money borrowed into a Sinking Fund, either (1) by an equal annual instalment of principal alone, with a gradually decreasing sum for interest on the principal for the time being unpaid ;or (2) by equal instal- ments of interest and principal combined by way of annuity, i.e. the total amount of interest during the 60 years is calculated and added to the principal, and 1-60th of the total amount is repaid each year during the term. It must be quite clear to any of you that if the latter mode of repay- ment is adopted, the annual sums payable during the first few years of the loan are much less than they would be under tbe first method. The exact difference is pointed out by Mr. Tunstall in his re- port. By the first method, the payment during the first three years would be, respectively, .£13,471, .£13.323, and £13,174, as against.by the other method, £10,639 10s., during each year of the loan. It is proposed by the Corporation to establish a Sinking Fund by the latter mode, so as to relieve the pre- sent ratepayers, as far as possible, from any addi- tional charge upon the rates. Without providing for any increase in the revenue of the undertaking, or the rateable value of the Borough, Mr. Tunstall states that the increase upon the rates would not exceed 30. in the .£, and that if the Water Works revenue increased at the same rate during the next three years, as it did in the last three, the charge upon the rates would be respectively, 2id., 2d., and id., in the If, however, the Corporation obtain a suspension of the Sinking Fund for three years. the increase in the Water revenue and in the rateable value of the Borough would possibly provide against any addi- tional charge upon the rates.

div.head: MANUFACTURERS' SUPPLY.
div.p: THE MANUFACTURERS' SUPPLY.

Some years ago, the Corporation, with the object of relieving • several large manufacturers from the difficulty of providing themselves with a proper supply of water, permitted three of the largest companies in the town to lay mains under the public streets of the borough to enable them to supply their works with water from the river. Objection was taken to the purchase of the Water Works principally by those manufacturers who feared that their supply from the River Mersey might be interfered with. The Corporation were not blind to the importance of this supply of water to those manufacturers, nor to the value of the prosperity of those works to, the welfare of the Borough—works employing between 3,000 and 4,000 people, and contributing a large rateable value and supporting a large section of trades people of all classes in the Borough. The manufacturers on their part were alive to the value of this water supply, and I am happy to tell you that we have agreed with these manufacturers to in- sure their permanent right to this supply, they paying us £3,000, by three annual instalments,and a way leave rate of 3d. per yard according to :the length of streets used. This sum on Mr. Tunstall's figures will meet any deficiency chargeable against the rates. The purchase was admitted by the speakers at the Ratepayers' Meeting to be a desirable one, the only objection being to the time when effecting it, whether this or next year, and on that point the Corp)ration assures you that it could not be acquired on any terms so advantageous next year as the present one.

div.head: INCREASE OF -THE LIBRARY RATE.
div.p: INCREASE OF -THE LIBRARY RATE.

Objection was taken to fixing the maximum rate to be authorized for the Library and Museum at 2d. The Council have considered this, and have decided to agree toreduce the rate from 21. to lid. when the Bill is in Committee. This entirely does away with the opposition on that ground, and,seeing that the Lending Library will be free, I trust that all interested will consequently vote in favour of that portion of the Bill. OTHER, OBJECTIONS.

The clauses relating to the charges for the tem- porary shelter of persons suffering from infectious diseases, and to the closing of the I,ark on special occasions, will be altogether abandoned from the Bill. Now, I have only to conclude by urging you in your own interests and in the interests of the town generally, to fill up your voting paper for the poll in favour of the Bill. (Cheers). Alderman SUTTON, who had now taken the 'place of the Mayor (who had to go to another meeting) said he hoped they would all bear in mind the one

div.head: EXAMINER, SATUIDAN4 MARCH 29, 1890.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATUIDAN4 MARCH 29, 1890.

fact—that there was no one of them, so far as he knew, who was personalky or pecuniarly interes, ed in this question, and therefore it could be of no benefit to any of them to ask the meeting to consent to that Bill. Everyone of them must exercise their own discretion and their own good judgment as to whether the Bill should be proceeded with or not. (Hear, hear.) Mr. F. DixoN asked if they were going to receive 0,000 from the manufacturers. Alderman SurroN : Yes.
Mr. F. DIXON said that in that case they would be going to the poll under altogether different circum- stances.

Alderman Surrox said that was only an informal meeting, and they would have to go to a poll under any circumstances, but at the last meeting several objections were made to clauses in the Bill. The Corporation had considered those objections and had come to the conclusion that they could fairly withdraw all the points to which those objections were raised. Alderman Sutton then explained the arrangement (as previously published by us) the Corporation proposed to make with the three firms of manufacturers as to their water supply. Mr. Dixon. could not understand why on earth the Cor- poration wanted to put burdens on the back of the three manufacturers. How many of these liability companies were paying any dividend? Yet the Corporation wanted to put new burdens on these firms. Ile did hope they would, have the common-sense not to do anything of the kind. The manufacturers of the town had had sufficient difficulties and troubles during the past fifteen years. Mr. Dixon next made an allusion to the gas supply, and then, speaking with regard to sanitary matters, he said n• one could get up and say they had been a success, except as far as the spending of money was concerned. (Applause.) What had the intercepting depots done? (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Mr. S. Barlow, interrupting in a loud voice, said : Mr. Chairman, I think our time is being taken up too much with this blether. (Much laughter.) - -

Mr. DIXON expressed a hope that working-men would fill up their voting papers against the Bill. They should lose nothing by deferring it till November,and then mak- ing it a municipal matter. (Applause.) Alderman Surrox informed Mr. Dixon and the meet- ing that the manufacturers approached the Corporation, and not the Corporation the manufacturers. He would ask Mr. T. Birchall, as representing one of the firms in- volved, to say a few words in regard to the matter. Mr. Dixon, he added, seemed to blame the Corporation for saving the ratepayers' money. (Hear, hear.) Mr. BIRCHALL said that he was sure that the manufac- turers would be obliged to Mr. Dixon, but perhaps it would have been better had he let them speak for them- selves. (Hear, hear.) At first the White Cross Com- pany, Pearson and Knowles Company, and Messrs. Ry-lands Bros., felt somewhat aggrieved, and thought that their privileges, the rights which they had fairly acquired, should not be interfered with. They felt also that the proposed Bill might mean a serious addition to the rates. About twelve years ago the firms mentioned had frequently to stop their manufacture owing to the ; want of water. The Water Works Company had then I only the Appleton supply, and there was nothing for it but for the manufacturers to go to the river. They did so, and incurred a very great outlay, and when the present Bill was proposed they naturally thought they had a right to approach the Corporation with regard to the continuance tithe supply. The result was the arrangement that had been arrived at for the payment of £3,000, in three yearly instalments, and for the payment of a way-leave of 3d. per yard for the passage of their pipes through the streets. The sum of £3,000 that they would pay would prevent a deficiency I in the rates. That obstacle out of the way, they did not ' see why they,should oppose the purchase. The Bill in its entirety was a very valuable one, and the extension of the borough was an important matter. (Ap- plause.) Councillor MONKS (interrupting) asked whether any terms for the purchase had been arranged, whether any report had been made, and whether the Corporation as a whole had considered the matter for five minutes since the last ratepayers' meeting? Alderman SUTTON answered " 'yes." The Corporation had considered the matter for many five minutes. His opinion was that any member of the Council who had not considered the Bill for himself, and considered it

fully— Councillor MONKS: That is not my question. I put a plain question. I asked you whether the terms of purchase— Alderman HARRISON: I rise to a point of order. I do not think Mr. Bircnall is being fairly used. _ .

• - 1*- Mr. BIRCHALL then continued Ps remarks, and said that if the Water Works were not purchased now a higher price would have to be paid for them were they bought in the future. Alderman Sorrow mentioned that he personally had attended three special meetings of the General Purposes Committee, summoned expressly for the purpose of con- sidering the Bill, and one special meeting of the Council, summoned for the same purpose.

_ Councillor MONKS said that the Committee meetings the Alderman referred to had been held to consider the terms with the manufacturers, and a special meeting was held to confirm those terms and to consider the library rate. But in regard to the purchase of the Water Works, nothing had been done since the meeting at which they were asked to confirm the Bill. The price of the Water Works they did not know, of the condition of the undertaking they had had no report, and for any- thing they knew the Corporation, after the ratepayers had given assent to the Bill, might purchase at any price they thought proper, without considering the ratepayers at all. He warned his fellow-townsmen against passing the

Bill. He did not believe that the Corporation had legallY incurred £2OO in expenses. If any officials, or set of officials, had chosen to act illegally, it was their own affair, but for himself he did not believe that £2OO had been legally incurred in regard to the Bill. The Borough Treasurer, he knew, would not pay one halfpenny of the expenditure until he and the Council were satisfied that the charges were perfectly legal. He did not object to the purchase of the Water Works, and believed that ' with the terms offered, provided that the reports of the condition of the works, and the finances, were satisfac- tory, it might turn out to be on the whole a very profit- able affair for the town. Until he knew the terms that would be accepted by the Company, and until he was satisfied as to the condition of the plant upon a better opinion than his own, he was not prepared to support the spending of a quarter of a million of the money of the ratepayers. (Applause.) He was not going to object to the gift of £3,000, but that did not in any way alter the purchase. If they threw out the Bill they need not stop one single day in negotiating for the purchase of the works, as they could do it under present Acts. He was satisfied they would not get the Bill. He was told that the Parliamentary Committee of the County Council intended to- oppose it, and that the Local Government Board intended to oppose it, and they had no enthusiasm either in the town or the Council to support the Bill. (Applause.) He was in favour of deferring the matter until more inquiry could be made, and until they could move unitedly. (Applause.) - - -- •

Mr. JoinT Wataits said that the objections Mr. Monks took at the first meeting of ratepayers had been con- sidered on all sides, and the Bill had been amended in consequence. His objections had been considered and removed, and he now complained that the Bill was in a muddle. If they found that certain clauses of the Bill were not suitable to them as ratepayers, their business was to make objection, and if the Corporation thought fit to drop the clauses, that was a fair course to take, and he thanked the Corporation for having regard to the expressed wishes of the ratepayers. They agreed with Mr. Monks that the opinion ot experts must be sought before the Water Woes purchase was entered up- on. Was anyone prepared to give either thirty or twenty years' purchase until the opinion of the experts was known? Personally, he decidedly objected to anything of the kind, and he took the Corporation to be perfectly sincere when they said that no agreement would be entered upon until they had had an inspection of the plant and the books. That meeting was not held to absolutely confirm the Bill in all its particulars, and they would not commit, themfelves to thirty years' purchase. ' If the property proved on inspection not to be what they I had thought, they would decline the purchase. What was wanted was that they should give the Council power to move. Mr. Monks said they could purchase the Works without obtaining a 13111. So they could, but they could not obtain the statutory powers which the Company possessed without a Bill, and those powers were simply invaluable to the Corporation. Councillor Moine : I have asked the Town Clerk— because Mr. Whittle is our Town Clerk new—(applause) —and he says we can purchase the works as we exist without this Bill.

Mr. WALKER : I have explained you caa purchase just as you can purchase any works, but unless you have a Bill you cannot acqure anything but the plant and property. You cannot acquire the statutory powers. Councillor MONKS) : I wish to make the purchase, and then go to Parliament to confirm it. - - - •

Mr. WALKER, continuing, asked why the Bill should be delayed ? They, had already spent £l,OOO. If Mr. Monks thought it had not been spent legally, he should be glad if he would go into the matter. The money had been spent, and the chances were that the ratepayers would have to pay it. After going three-fourths of the way, they would be a parcel of noodles not to go forward without good reason could be shown for turning back. Unfortunately, Mr. Monks was interested, and could not help it, because his works were just beyond the present boundaries. He was unavoidably interested id the matter,and a delay to him necessarily meant thesaving of some money. He did not say that was a leading motive with Mr. Monks ' • he did not believe it was, but it was a stock rule with magistrates, for instance, that they should not sit upon a case in which they were interested. AU the difficulties Mr. Monks had raised could easily be dealt with during the next twelve months, and the pre- sent Bill would really extend over that period. As they were getting all that they could reasonably desire, they would only be acting like reasonable men if they voted for the Bill. (Applause.)

Mr. W. El. BUTLER said it seemed to be assumed that the only use for water was to put it into steam boilers, but he was more concerned with the quality of the water for individual use. From "The Examiner" supplement, he found that an analysis was made in 1888, but it was spoken of in such general terms that he wished to ask if the Corporation were prepared to submit to the meeting an analysia of the water, so that they could judge how it stood as, compared with the water of other towns.

Alderman Surrox : We have it on the highest authority that there is no better water to be obtained anywhere for domestic purposes than the Winwick water. Mr. T. /Amara said that during the last few days the General Purposes Committee of the Corporation had so altered and amended :the Bill that every objection he could have raised against it had been met. Mr. Dixorz.—ls the speaker a ratepayer? The CHAIRMAN said these interruptions were unseemly and disrespectful. Mr. WizmAx ROM/MTS.-It is an insult. Mr. MORRIS said he was a ratepayer. It was because it had been realized that, when the Corporation became sellers of water they could fill up the pipes which the manufacturers who drew water from the river were now
SHOPPING IN SEDAN CHARLOTTE'S 'VISIT' tpeproduction

using, the manufacturers met the GenerSl Purposes Committee and made them an offer. Now, he asked that meeting, were they all agreed as ratepayers that the Water Works should be in the hands of the Corporation. (" No; no," "Yes.") Was it not a well-known fact that municipal bodies ought to hold, not only the Water Works, but the gas properties? (Hear, hear.) If they were agreed upon that point, it resolved itself into a question of cost. The longer the purchase was delayed the bigger the price would be. Hence he said to the ratepayers, " If this is a good property "—and if it was not they had no occasion to buy it—" buy it." (Hear, hear.) As it was a growing concern, it was better to buy it now than wait 12 months or two years. (Applause.)

Alderman HARRISON said that if there were any clause in the Bill to which exception might be taken the rate- payers had the power to have it remedied when before a Committee of the House of Commons. In justice to Councillor Monks, he might say that he believed that a selfish motive would be one of the,very last by which he would be actuated—(applause)--for he had heard Councillor Monks say' distinctly, on more than one occasion in the Council, that whether it was to his inter- est or not he should feel it his duty to support an extension of the boundaries; notwithstanding the fact that it would include his works in it, and they were not at the present time in the borough. If the ratepayers concluded Ito purchase the Water Works, it was distinctly under- stood that a proper examination would be made, and an expert called in, with the view of ascertaining whether the works were calculated to do all that they appeared to be capable of doing, whether they w,ould yield such a supply and quality of water as to keep up the dividend which was being earned and which had been steadily increasing for several years past. The proper test of value was not to examine the plant or the quality of water so much as to look at the company's last report and see what their dividend was. If the ratepayers bought the works now, they would buy them to an advantage which perhaps a year or two would utterly destroy. He believed • the ratepayers of Warrington would act wisely if they supported the action of the Council by voting in favour of the Bill. ("No, no," and applause.)

Mr. WILLIAM DIGOLE said that if tho matter were delayed for a year or two the ratepayers would be better, instead of worse off. There had recently been a great increase of cottage property in Latchford and the neighbourhood, due to the construction of the Ship Canal. When that work was completed, the occupation of a great many of those houses would cease, inasmuch as there were no projected works in that district, neither were there ever likely to be any. Rents would go down, the assessments would have to follow, and so the income of the Water Company would be reduced. He was, however, in favour of the purchase Of the works for the reason that no private company should have anything to do with the stieets. What he wanted the ratepayers to do was to buy the Water Works at the market value, but to test the quality of the water, and that, it would be found, would depreciate the price. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Moms There is no city or town in the universe that has water to snit all domestic and ,manufacturing purposes. Mr. SAMUEL BARLOW contended that 30 years' pur- chase was too much to pay for the works. Councillor FLEmimo said he thought it only fair that the Corporation should have approached the Water Works Company in the manner they had done, rather than by the alternative mode of compulsion. (Hear, hear.) So far as the extension of the borough was con- cerned, it would be to the interest of Warrington to extend its boundaries. The town would grow, and in time to come the water would be 25 per cent. cheaper. For Heaven's sake let them go on with the Bill, and pos- terity would bless them. (Applause.) , _ Mr. WILLIAM ROBERTS said he thought the members of the Council had met the ratepayers in a proper and conciliatory spirit, and those ratepayers who were at first opposed to that matter ought in return to meet the Council in the same spirit; because it must be remem- bered that the Council had but one object in view—the good of the ratepayers. He was glad to be able to say not a single member of the Council who had prominently supported the purchase was a large shareholder of the Water Works Company. On the other hand, he had found that several of the prominent opponents of the purchase were large shareholders. (Hear, hear.) that was a very significant fact, and it showed that there was a motive in urging the ratepayers to delay this matter. As a small ratepayer he urged the meeting to support the Corporation in carrying the Bill. (Hear, hear, and "No, no.")

Mr. Joux MAGTNN remarked that nothing, had been said of the benefit the ratepayers would derive from the purchase. They had been told that it was cheap enough, and was even a great bargain, but where would the rate- payers get benefit for the rates they were likely to have to pay? (Hear, hear.) How had the Water Works Company obtained their maximum dividend? In the first place, the Corporation had paid larger bills for water, within the six months ending December last, than ever they had paid; in the second place. the Water Works Company had not spent a penny on their works or plant; and, in the third place they had not put a shilling to the reserve fund. (Applause.) When the Corporation had secured that great, good bargain, was it likely that the works would last for ever? Or would there not have to be a reserve fund? (Hear, hear.) The ratepayers had been told that the water rate would not exceed 3P. or 4d. in the £, but there was such a rate as the improvement rate, and the increase would be put upon that. They proposed to take over a liability of £27,000 for mortgages, and a further liability of £B,OOO, which, he argued, would bring the purchase to one of thirty-five years. He advised ratepayers to vote against the Bill. (Applause.)
