11/4 Mr. G. Wat.manroa said they ought to .have pur- chased the Water Works five-and-twenty yeare the late Mr. Peter Rylauds proposed to do It, 'Ma grBat opponent of it at the time was their friend who hoe% just died (Mr. McMinnies), and he had tinge said the Mitt 'st , mistake he had ever made was when he opposed the pas - chase of the Water Works-, and the Gas Works. (ew, hear.) They should find they had again made a ham mistake if they did not nosy purchase the Water Works. (Hear, hear.) He was quite willing to take his share of any burden that might be inetared. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Join; Wesaan, in replyirstr to Mi. Magi's state- ment that themoney to be paid to the Water Works Company was more like 35 years' purchase of their dividend than 323'years, pointed out that the £27.Pore- ferred to by Mr, 3faginre was mortgage money, and the interest upon this mortgage was paid out of the revenue of the Company. The revenue of the Conipany was really larger than the £B,OOO upon which the Corporation based their thirty years' purchase. The interest upon that £27,000 was paid out of the gross revenue, but the Corporation were only asked to pay thirty years' purchase en the net revenue—that was to say, on the revenue that was left after the interest on this mortgage had been paid. The actual earnings of the Company were over £9,000. If the £27,000 had been; in share capital, in- stead of a mortgage, the Company would have been paying dividend upon it, and the Corporation in buying the Water Works would have had to pay thirty years' purchase on that dividend. The very fact that that £27,000 was in mortgage, instead of in shares, was an actual saving to the Corporation in purchasing the Water Works. (Hear, hear.) With regard to the question of fire, the town was in this condition to-day, that if a big fire were to break out Warrington might be burned down. The Water Works Company wculd be very glad to put down larger mains, and give increased pressure. They would spend £lO,OOO, £15,000 or £20,000, and when the Corporation came to purchase they would have, to repay that £20,000 at thirty years' purchase on the extra dividend. As a matter of fact the Water Works Company were anxious that the Corporation should ask them to spend more money be- cause they knew the town would have to pay them for it in the end. As to the sewers, Warrington lay in a flat country and there was not a town in the country whose sewers stood more in need of flushing. Years ago Dr. Mackie said that if they could only open the sewers' of Warrington in the summer time they would find them to be great long cesspools. What the sewers required was flushing; but that could not be done because they had to pay for every gallon of water, and if the Corporation spent £lOO on water for flushing the sewers or for baths it meant that they would pay thirty times that MOO when they came to purchase the Water Works. (Hear, hear.) Why should they go on in that mad way?. If they had been wise enough twenty years ago to purchase the Water Works they would have saved the town £lOO,OOO, and if they left that purchase over for another twenty years they would have to pay another £lOO,OOO. (Hear, hear.) He said stop that monopoly. Let the natural increment on the Water Works go into the pockets of the ratepayers, and let them not put another £lOO,OOO into the pockets of the Water Works Company. (Ap- plause.)

I Mr. KIERNAN suggested that the meeting should be adjourned so that the matter could be still further con- sidered, and perhaps they would get another £3,000 from the manufacturers. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Councillor W. PIERPOINT proposed a vote of thanks to Alderman Sutton for presiding. It had been said by some gentlemen that that Bill had been sprung upon the town, and that asssrtion had been endorsed by his friend, ex-Councillor Dixon, but if ex-Councillor Dixon knew what he was talking about and would take the trouble to examine the year books of the Corporation, he would find that on several occasions during the last two or three years the question of a Bill for the extension of the borough boundary had been mooted. (Hear, hear.) With reference to the manufacturers of Warrington he pointed out that, of their own free will, they offered £3,000 for the purpose of promoting the Bill, and that was because they felt their own interests were so bound up with the Bill. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The Bill meant that the town would have a Free Library. It would mean also an extension of the borough boundary, which was greatly to be desired. If they did not get the Bill this year the subject would drop, and he had no hesitation in saying that it would not be mooted again during the next ten years. He concluded by moving a , vottof thanks to Alderman Sutton for presiding. The vote of thanks to Alderman Sutton was then agreed to with acclamation, and that gentleman having responded, the meeting terminated. •, -,=="
FATAL QUARREL BiLWEEN BROTHERS-

div.head: IN-LAW.
div.p: IN-LAW.

Mr. Samuel Haywood, a member of the Ashby Wold Local Board, during a quarrel about half-past seven on Monday morning with his brother-in-law, was stabbed by the latter, and died immediately. The dispute is stated to have arisen from the fact that the alleged murderer did not work on Sunday. The deceased, who was a brick maker, was only on Monday morning to be nominated for the Ashby Board of Guardians.

div.head: ALARMING EXPLOSION.
div.p: ALARMING EXPLOSION.

An alarming explosion occurred at Dorchester, on Tuesday morning. Quartermaster-sergeant Howard, of Major Wallace's Battery of the Royal Horse Artillery, stationed in the town, was in the magazine getting am- munition for the firing practice when, from an unknown cause, the building was suddenly blown up with terrific force. Howard was rescued from the ruins as speedily as possible and removed to the military hospital, where lie was found to be so terribly injured that it is feared he cannot recover. The magazine was blown to pieces, some of the fragments being hurled to a great distance. The shock was felt throughout the town.

div.head: LLA.NERCH DISASTER.
div.p: THE LLA.NERCH DISASTER.

The inquiry into the Llanerch pit disaster was re- sumed on Tuesday. The manager expressed the opinion that the explosion occurred in Ne. 4 heading, or from the lights of the men working above in No. 3 heading. There were, he believed, several explosions as the result of the first explosion. The men were opposed to the use of locked lamps, but after such a disaver he should not think of working the pit with naked lights. The inquiry was adjourned. On Wednesday the inquiry concluded. The jury re- turned a verdict that the explosion originated in No. 4 heading from an outburst of gas, and that there was no evidence proving anyone blamable; but the' strongly recommended the use of locked lamps in the pit.

div.head: SURVIVORS OF BALACLAVA.
div.p: THE SURVIVORS OF BALACLAVA.

The following unsatisfactory letter has been received by Mr. L. Flood, of Manchester, who has interested himself in the welfare of several sur- vivors of Balaclava who are in an impoverished condition :

War Office, Pall Mall, March 214 1890 Sir,—ln reply to your letter of the 6th inst., bringing to his special notice the claims of the survivors of the Balaclava charge who are in indigent circumstances, I am directed by the Secretary of State for War to explain to you that the grant of soldiers' pensions is strictly governed by Royal Warrant, and that it would be im- possible to grant pensions or to increase them outside the terms of the warrant in favour of men who have taken part in any particular engagement. Such a con- cession would involve the grant of special pensions in all cases of soldiers who have taken part in famous or important battles, irrespective of the service they may have actually rendered to the State. Under these circum- stances, Mr. Secretary Stanhope regrets that he is unable ' to entertain the suggestion that a special pension should be provided for the pensioners who took part in the Bala- clava charge.—l am, sir, your obedient servant. Taos. C. B. CAVE, Mr. Lawrence Flood, Crosby Hotel, Manchester.

div.head: DEATH 01.. THE DUKE OFWANCHESTER, K.P.
div.p: DEATH 01.. THE DUKE OFWANCHESTER, K.P.

r The death of the Duke of Manchester, occurred at Naples on Friday evening. The Duchess of Manches- ter was with her husband at his death. The late William Drogo Montagu, Duke and Earl of Manchester, Viscount Mandeville, and Baron Montagu of Kirtibolton, in the peerage of Great Britain, was the eldest son of George, sixth Duke, by his first wife, • Millicent, daughter and heir of the late General Robert Bernard Soarrow, by Lady Olivia Acheson, and was born 15th October, 1823, consequently was in his 67th year. He married in July, 1852, Countess Louise Frederica Augusta von Alien, of Hanover, by whom he leaves two sons and three daugh- ters. His eldest son, George Victor Drogo, Viscount Mandeville, who succeeds to the dukedom, Was born in 1653, and married in 1876 Consuelo, daughter of Senor Antonio Yzuaya del Valle, of Revenswood, Louisiana, U.S.A., by whom he has a young family. Has younger son, Lord Charles Montagu, was born in lam and his , daughters are the Duchess of Hamilton, the Countess of Gos ford, and Lady Alice Stanley. erahe "Star" says:—" The nation scM hear with a thrill of respectful gratitude of the newest accession to its hereditary legislators, for it has heard of "Kim," alias the new Duke of Manchester, before. As Lord Mande- ville he has figured more than once in the courts, and has been the subject of innumerable paragraphs. A good- natured spendthrift, misled, it is said, by bad com- panions, the new Duke has almost beaten the record for sheer wildness. He has travelled, and accomplished one or two adventures out of the common. He is said to be not without talent or good in:tint/sea."

, The Mr. DrsnAma tried to solve tlis'„ f New Irish problem of the representation O Land Bill the people by what Caine V° be, known as a Fancy Franchise Bill. Mr. Balfour like him in one respect ; he seeks to settle a gre's: difficulty—the agrarian difficulty—by a 'll3clc, Land Purchase Bill. We should like to be in - position to conclude that this new fancy Ineasiir: will have a fate like unto that of prototype---tt is to say that the Irish Land Purchase Bill will turned inside out, and so licked into shape a's result in a really excellent piece of legislation' But we are afraid this is more than can be expected, for Mr. Balfour is neither so clever, pliant, nor so far-seeing 1.6 the late leader of the Tory party. It is something, however, that lie makes an ingenious, and what we believe to be an honest attempt to grapple with a most core' plicated question. Unfortunately, his scherae i 5 as complicated as the question itself—more enl/1: plicated, Mr. Gladstone remarked, than that o' any other scheme he had known. Not 3 fesill screens are put up to hide the fact that the whef plan rests upon pledging British credit to an au- vance of THIRTY-THREE MILLIONS of money t° buy out such of the Irish landlords as are to sell. Beyond this, John Bull requires to into account the TEN MILLIONS for which he has already become responsible under the bourne Act ; so that the proposal is to CO the country to a circulating sum of Foarv-TOll% MiLtrois s on helitdf of the landlords and at tenant farmers of Ireland. It is as well to ,n this, and to remember the outcry that was throughout the country by the Tories when GLADSTONE proposed to pledge British credit v"

the extent of FIFTY MILLI°Ns. It may be that the Tories have seen the error eft their ways, and are now bringing forth fruit rase for repentance. But they will have to ooderg: the ordeal of public opinion, and public opinie will, we cannot but think, strongly condemn sow; portions of the new bill. For instance, part of security for the repayment of the money advanou consists of the Imperial contributions otherwise set aside for education, and for poor law pull:oses. Now why, under any conceivable circumstalloseSc; should Martin in one part of a county be dePriv of assistance in the education of his children be- cause Patrick, living in another part of the ears° county, has proved thriftless, incompetent, or lor fortunate, and cannot pay his way under the and purchase clauses? And sO', with regard t° funds for Poor Law puiposes ; they ought to be held sacred for the object for which they are signed, and should not be liable to have currents turned awry" in order that they rees; trickle into the hands of Irish landlords. 01 measure, it should be added, is described as Bill to provide further fa4ties for the purchase!: land in Ireland, for the improvement of the colic; ; tion of the poorer and more congested distrie...4 and for the constitution of a Land Departmel°

We must confess to a liking for the proposal to con- folidate the various authorities acting in Ireland into a single Land Department; for, if properly carried out, centralisation in a matter of this kind will result in greater energy and greater economy. The relief of congested districts is imperative; but We are afraid Mr. BALFOUR is not the man to ac- oomplish the work. He has, however, shown bold- bess in one respect, and that as in the suggestion that the sum of one million and a half of the residue of the Irish Church Surplus Fund should be applied for this part of his scheme. It could carcely be applied to better purposes, and we wel- 'come the proposal even if it should prove nothing more than an object lesson to those who have an eye 'on the national property at present in the hands of the English Church. Leave was immediately given to introduce the Bill, which was read for the first tir!le on Monday. The second reading was fixed for the 14th April, and meantime the British taxpayer Would do well to read, mark, learn and inwardly digest it.

Toryism IN the House of Commons, on in Tuesday evening, Mr. MUNDELLA Educat. lon. exposed the reactionary policy of the present Government as revealed in their administration of the Education Act. He moved

- That this House is of opinion that the action of the Education Department in reference to the 811PPIY of public school accommodation in the cities of York and Salisbury is contrary to the spirit and intention of the Education Act of 1870, and injurious to the interests of education." The case of Salisbury has been prominently before the public. There has been a School Board there (but no board School) for seventeen years. The school accommodation was unsatisfactory, and, in I)ecernber 1888, the Education Department wrote to the Salisbury Board pointing to the need of atePB being taken. Nothing was done—except tilat the Bishop began, as the pharse goes, to Move heaven and earth" to prevent a Board School being established. The Department, 41Stead of insisting, as the law requires, that the Salisbury School Board should do its AtiatY, looked on and countenanced ridiculous clay, so as to enable the Church party to caPY the field. Two British Schools were e'°Eted on the understanding that Board Schools Would take their place; but the end of the intrigue la that one of the schools is put into the hands of the Kilburn Sisters—Protestant nuns, we suppose they may be called—while the rest of the acconimo- tiation is to be met by a school to be erected by a Church Association. Excepting one Roman thOic S'chool, the whole of the schools in Sails- • Y vrill now be under the control of the Church Party. The injustice of this to Nonconformists is as flagrant as is the conspiracy of neglect on the Part of the Education Department. How if it had 4._becli a Roman Catholic Bishop who had been trying the strings to prevent the School Board doing clatY ? Does anybody suppose that the Govern- would in that case have waited over a year to et,ll: able him to "nobble " the school area? Not a "44-Jr it; and this shows how miserably one-sided allti reactionary is the policy which is being Zcii Ned. The case of York is as bad, or worse, for Icl'o the Government have allowed a Church 4ssociation to step in after a School Board had actually been established to supply the deficiency in aehnol accommodation. There was the same sort :5f delay—all with the object of playing into the of a sect. Mr. MuNDELLA, notwithstanding 'Ts strong case, did not carry his motion; it was 'created by a majority of 52. But beyond the Ilcalse of Commons there is the nation; and we ,ate certainly much mistaken if the nation will 'allg tolerate this wretched manceuvring between urch and State. In order to put an end to this r- a/neful partizanship, we must have education 'too and under popular control.

The voting papers will be collected on Mon- and by Tuesday it will be known whether 'fhere is a majority, and what the majority is, in :aur of the measure. However indifferent some Of the members of the Town Council may have 1, trwu themselves as to the provisions of the Bill, Zeve can be no question as to the keen interest I_l4/1 which it has been discussed by the inha.bi- -'‘lttil generally. Mr. DIXON far4illed to think it a great hardship that the menu- tn-rrers -should be called upon to pay anything; 67 the firms in question well know what they are tba -lit, and that they are getting full value for trir Money. This payment of £3,000 comes in e 'lick of time; and, as it converts formidable °1315 • °fleas into active supporters of the measure,. tv°Shall be very much surprised if the poll does ~. teVeal that there is a substantial majority in i41:°11 of the-Bill. Councillor Mowxs referred at te Public meeting, on Monday, to the opposition cLtile Lancashire County Council, and of the t cat Government Board; but we have every rea- ti:l to believe that the opposition of :411688t bodies will disappear upon their .101_44141g concessions which they are entitled 1 and which the Corporation will be pre- IL• ted to make. 'There was obviously, at the meet- til°4 Alonday, a better feeling towards the bill Atall has hitherto been manifested. div.head: " Touca AND GO."
div.p: " Touca AND GO."

India has anticipated England in producing a surplus; the income for the year exceeds the ex- penditure by £1,700,000. This is good; but we hope to have a larger surplus at home. In the new Budget for our great De.pendency,provision is made for increasing the duty on spirits; but it does not seem as if anything is to be done as to the salt duty. It ought to be reduced, with a view to its final abolition. Salt is a necessity, not a luxury. The Ltberal Union Club has decided to give a banquet to Lord Hartington on the 14th May. As Mr. Chamberlain is to preside, it is interesting to remember that there was a time when the member for West Birmingham described his lordship as Rip Van Winkle. Mr. Goschen ought to be there, for he was Mr. Chamberlain's Skeleton of the Feast, was he not? What a change since the days of the passionate advocacy of the Radical Programme!

"Hitch your wagon to a star" Emerson said. They have not yet quite got to that in America ; but they are about to hitch the wagon on to Niagara. A news item to hand says :—" The pro- posal of an American syndicate to lease the water power of the Falls for an electric factory has been abandoned, and that of an English syndicate with the same object accepted, 10,000dols. having been deposited to bind the contract."

The Welshmen in Warrington deserve helping in the efforts they are making to raise funds for building a Welsh Church, for as a people they always go to work by helping themselves. The Mayor did well, in presiding over the concert, on Monday evening, to state that in his Police Court experience as a magistrate he had never yet had a Welshman brought before him. A fact like this needs no comment; it speaks volumes.

The Tories have managed to win the Ayr Burghs by a majority of 130; and, if it will only have the effect of causing the Government to dis- solve in the belief that their fortunes are mending, it will be something for Liberals even to rejoice over. But it is to be feared they will look back to the last General Election, and perceive that their majority, which was then 1,175, is now 130 only; in other words, that since then it has been reduced by 1,045 votes.

At a meeting of the Browning Society, held yesterday at University College, London, Mrs. De Conroy Laffan read a paper on "The Beautiful Commonplaces of Browning." On the face of it, it would seem that that which is commonplace can have little or no connection with the beautiful; but poets have their own way of looking at things, and Shelley goes to the root of the matter when he says—" Familiar things grow beautiful through love.'

What is to be done with the brothers Davies— the Crewe parricides? Are they to be hanged, or imprisoned for life? The murder was one of the most revolting ever known ; and yet there is no denying that the conduct of the murdered man was also most revolting. The youths seem to have been worked up to a pitch bordering on insanity; they hated their father because of his cruelty to them- selves and their mother. But should they be hanged? That is the question; and it is a ques- tion upon which public opinion is very much divided.

Lord Dunraven has retired from the Chairman- ship of the Sweating Committee. It is understood that, Conservative though he is, he is quite Radical in his opinion as to the sweaters; and as he is overpowered by fossil members of the Committee he leaves them to their mild and meaningless ways. It is a credit to him that he has broken from them; we have hopes of Lord Dunraven.

The Labour Conference at Berlin is moving, it is rumoured, in the direction of limiting the hours of children and females, and of making provision for Sunday being more generally observed as a day of rest. This is all in the right direction so far as Continental labour is concerned. It may be no great advance upon what is now done in this country; but it will be something gained if steps are taken to place England and her foreign com- petitors on a footing of equality.

The labour question agitates the New World quite as much as the Old. We observe from a hand-bill which has reached us from Mr. Whitham that "there are now over 25,000 persons tramping the streets of San Francisco, looking for work that is not to be found." An attempt is being made to organize the unemployed with a view Co action " in a calm, dignified and orderly manner, worthy of American citizens." But it is insisted that "something must be done, and that some- thing done immediately:"

This labour problem is the problem of problems. It ought to be possible for every man to have work who wants to work. As population increases, the pressure becomes greater, and, although there may not be a larger per-centage of unemployed there is a larger number. It is simply horrible— this having, as Burns has it, "to beg a brother of the earth to give him leave to toil r But what is to be done ? " Ay ! there's the rub;" and yet we shall be compelled before many years are over to do something more than sigh, and drop the subject.

Speaking at a Primrose League meeting at Lymm, on Tuesday, Mr. J. W. D. Barron had his little say on labour matters as follows :—" If they would trace back to the source of those strikes they would find the socialistic element had much to do with them, the leaders caring little for the demo ralization of society and the stagnation of trade It was their duty to try and restore confidence between capital and labour." The moral of which is—

_ Bless the squire and his relations, And keep us in our proper stations. And quite the right sort of rubbish, too, to shoot at the poor creatures who sell their birthright for a cheap tea, and a nod now and again from a Knight or Dame of the Primrose League.

In the case of alleged drinking during prohibited hours at the "Ring o' Bells," Wilderspool-rd., en Sun- day week, three police officers gave evidence which, if true, rendered a conviction absolutely necessary. One witness only gave rebutting evidence; and yet the magistrates dismissed the case with the remark that, "although they thought the police officers had done their duty, they were inclined to give the defendant the benefit of the doubt". What must the police think in such a case? That the magistrates regard them as perjured witnesses ? " DO2O their duty" indeed ! Can it be the magistrates who have failed in their duty ? The township meetings are distinguishing them- selves. The Rev. Canon Dodd presided at 'the Stretton meeting, on Monday, and amongst other business transactei, it was announced that four- pence per dozen will be given in future for spar- rows killed in the township." Shakespere has Scriptural authority for his reference to Him— " that doth the ravens feed— Yea, providently caters for the sparrow." Can it be that the farmers of Stretton and their reverend Chairman understand these things better than Sliakespere—and Providence?

Anyhow, it is hard on the sparrows to be brought into the world for slaughter at the rate of four- pence per dozen, and we wish we could help them, too, in the struggle for existence. ," Ouida ' is re- garded as something of a heathen; but we are with her all the way, when, describing her heroine in "Follie-Farine," and referring to the birds, she 6 says:— • "She loved them; they and the four-footed beasts were the only things that did not flee from her; anal the woful and mad slaughter of them by the peasants was to her a grief passionate in its despair. She did not reason on what she felt; but to her a slain bird was a trust betrayed, an inno- cence defiled, a creature of heaven struck to earth." Canon Dodd should read this passage; it will set him thinking.

The London correspondent of the "Eastern Morning News" states that on Thursday afternoon, after the meeting with Lord Salisbury, the Chief Secretary made this announcement to a political' adherent. The issolu- tion is fixed for the autumn of next year, unless some unexpected event occurs to precipitate.

SPRING FASHIONS, Spring Fasidons.—J. & W. DUTTON, 16 and 18, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. MORE COAL ROBBERIES AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday. Mary Ann Stokes, of 17, Sankey-st., was charged with stealing 116 lbs. of coal, valued at 11d., the property of the Lon- don and North-Western Railway Co. P.C. Murray stated that on Wednesday he was on duty on the Old Marsh, when he saw the prisoner and three other women standing upon the buffers of a wagon which was loaded with coal. They were placing the coal into bags, but upon seeing him the women ran away. He succeeded in catching the prisoner. The four bags were nearly filled, and contained about 4cwt. of coal.—The prisoner, who had been four times convicted of theft, was sentenced to two months' hard labour. ALLEGED THEFT OF AN UMBRELLA AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. A. Thomas and Dr. Steele, Catherine Percival, a married woman, of Sutherland-st., was charged with having on the 17th inst., stolen an umbrella belonging to Samuel Spann, beerhouse keeper, Bentinck-st. On the date mentioned, Mr. Spann's daughter Fanny, aged 12 years of age, went to Mr. Buck's chemist shop in Bridge-st. While executing her errand she placed her umbrella against the counter, and after she had left the shop, she discovered that she had left her umbrella. She at once returned and from what Mr. Buck told tier, Ale went out and saw the prisoner walking up Bridge-st.. carry- ing the missing umbrella. The girl shouted but the pri- soner ran faster and became lost to view. Information was given to the police, and in the evening P.C. Wood- row visited the prisoner's house, accompanied by the girl, and as soon as the prisoner saw her, she exclaimed, "Oh, its the little girl that I took the umbrella from out of Buck's shop." The defence was that the umbrella was taken not with the intention of stealing it. but with the intention of returning it to the owner, and that the prisoner looked about for the girl but could not find her. Mr. J. Burton, who defended, was prepared to call wit- nesses, but the magistrates intimated that they did not think there was sufficient evidence to convict, and the prisoner was discharged. PRESENTATION TO MAJOR 13RTINNER, OF WIDNES. After drill on Tuesday evening, the members of the Widnes companies of the 2nd Volunteer Battadon of the South Lancashire Regiment, presented to Major Brunner, an electro-plated mineral cruet, in recognition of his services to the volunteer cause in Widnes. The cruet bore a suitable inscription. Captain Lewis,who presided, drew attention to the fact that Major Brunner connected himself with the volunteer movement in 1873, when the Widnes companies were formed, and at once took com- mand of the H Company. He held that command until last year, when he felt bound to sever his connection with them. During the whole of the time he had been connected with the movement, the officers and men felt that they had in Major Brunner a personal friend, and it was a mattet of great regret, both at head quarters and at Widnes, that Major Brunner had withdrawn from active command.—Colour-Sergeants Burns and Davies then handed the present to Major Brunner, who, in acknowledging the gift, said he looked upon the time he had spent as a volunteer officer, both at range, camp,and other places as among the happiest which he had spent during his long Connection with Widnes. Ile spoke of the importance of the volunteer movement, and what would be renuired of volunteers, in case of invasion, in defence of their country. He urged them to increase their numbers in Widnes, and perfect themselves in the duties they undertock. In saying good-bye to them they had both collectively and individually his best wishes for their future success, not only as volunteers, but as men intheir various capacities.

BETHESDA CONOREGATIONAL CHAPEL, RUNCORN. The annual tea party in connection with this place of worship, was held in the schoolroom, on Wednesday evening. An excellee. tea was provided, and several of the ladies of the congregation presided over the tables and attended to the wants of the numerous. guests. Subsequently a concert was given under the presidency of Mr. W. 11. Chadwick, who delivered an appropriate speech in opening the pniceedings. In the course of the evening the Rev. John Simpson. of Stockport. who has been invited to undertake the pastorate of Bethesda, gave art address, in which he dealt with several phases of church work. The rev. gentleman had a most cordial reception. The musical programme was entirely carried , otit by the choir, under the conductorship of Mr. J. Clough, who also accompanied on the plane. The choir rendered' with good effect,the anthems "Now lift our joyful songs," "Sing, 0 ye heavens," and" In Jewry is God known,' also the selection from St. Paul, "130 W lovely arethe messengers." The chorus, "Then they ran upon him. was also capitally sung, Mr. Worrell taking the solo. The other, items on the prorramme were song, ‘• Edith," Miss Barrow; song, " Too Late," Miss Heatherington song, " T'ween Decks," Mr. Gornlock : song, "The Lost Chord," Miss Gandy; and solo' "Com- fort ve my people." Mr. Gornloek and Mr. Worrell were honoured with encores, and a similar compliment was paid to Mr. Clifford Le Couteur fop a brilliantly exe- cuted pianoforte solo After the concert a salt of work was held with the object of clearing off the debt incurred by the repairing and renovation of the organ of the chapel. Tho stall, which was laden with fancy and use- ful articles, the product of the deft fingers of the -mem- bers of the Ladies' Sewing Class,was in charge of Mrs. T. Handley, Mrs. A. Cameron, Miss Williams, Miss Maude Littler, Miss Nellie Handley, Miss C. Handley, and Miss Holliday. ``The sales realized about £lO, which was coq- rl-red luihlv satisfactory. On the proposition of Mr. T Handley, seconded by Mr. J. Slade, a vote of thanks was accorded to all who had taken part in the evening's ' proceedings.

FJOTBALL MATCH AT WIDNES.

On Thursday afternoon a match was played at Widnes, between Widnes first fifteen and Mr. Crotnpton's Runcorn team, which was principally composed of members of the" A" team. A large number of specta- tors had an opportunity of watching a capital game, which ended in a victory for the home team by 1 goal 2 tries and 1 miner, to Runcorn 1 goal to 3 minors. Clarke, Peters and Stubbs scored the tries for Widnes, and Crompton drovped the goal for the visitors.

div.head: MAD DOG AT LARGE AT DITTON,
div.p: MAD DOG AT LARGE AT DITTON,

_ Shortly after noon on Tuesday, much excitement was eaused lathe districts of Ditton and Hale, inconsequence of the appearance of a large black retriever dog showing signs of madness. Sergeant Ross, P.C. Townley, and Mr. Thomas Leather, a local buteliiir. went armed with a gun in search of the dog, and after hunting about a considerable time, they found it in a field, there behav- ing in a very suspicious manner, and apparently para- lysed in its hind legs. ' The dog made away to Hale village, where he was captured and brought back to Mr. Halsall's farm and shot by Mr. Leather: A post-mortem examination Of the dog's body will be made.

RUNCORN INDUSTRIAL BUILDING SOCIETY. This society, which is ccnducted on the ballot and sale principle,iad an appropriation by ballot on Tuesday evening last,at the society's office, No. 10, High-st., Run- corn, Mr. John Poole presiding. The minutes of the previous appropriation meeting were confirmed. Messrs. R. Wainwright and George Shone were appointed scrutineers, and the process of balloting having been explained, the ballot was proceeded with, resulting in registered number 4, belonging to the book held by Mr. Daniel Worthington, of Brackley-et., Runcorn, and representing two £lOO shares, being drawn. Mr. Worthington being clear on the society's books was declared entitled to an advance of £2OO free of interest, to be repaid at the rate of 8 per cent. per annum. A vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman for presid- ing. FIRE AT RUNCORN.

About nine c'clock on Tuesday night, a fire was dis- covered in the stock room of Mr. J. A. Smith, pawn- broker, of Alcock-st., and alarm was immediately given. The fire brigade were on the scene in the space of a quarter of an hour, but by this time the fire had ob- tained p. firm hold of the building, and it was feared would spread to adjoining property. The brigade, however,,under the command of Superintendent R. Wright and deputy superintendent W., Wright, directed three jets of water with great judgment, and succeeded in confining the flames to one portion of the building, and saved a large number of pledges, of which the stock consisted. The stockroom consisted of two cottages, and with the exception of the walls one of these was com- pletely demolished. The'datnage is estimated at about £l,OOO, and is covered by insurance.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO A RUNCORN UnD.rELL.OW. . .
div.p: PRESENTATION TO A RUNCORN UnD.rELL.OW. . .

--- For a period of 25 years Mr. Robert Wright has occu- pied the position of treasurer to Loyal William IV. Lodge of the Manchester Unity Order of Oddfellows, Runcorn, and the members have recently acknowledged this long servitude by presenting Bro. Wright, P.P.G.M.,• with a gold pendant. On one side of the pendant is inscribed the motto of the order, and en the reverse are the words, "Presented to P.P.G.M. Robert Wright by the Loyal William IV. Lodge 1085 1.0. of O.M.U. ,as an acknowledg- ment of his valuable services for over 25 years." P.P G.M. T. Cook made the presentation in a neat speech, and 13r0. Wright, in replying, said he had been 37 years in Run- corn and for 38 years he had been a member of the lodge. When he undertook the office of treasurer 25 years ago, the credit balance was £823 the value of the Lodge at the end of last year was £1,748. He concluded by cordi- ally thanking the members for their gift.

TOWNSHIP MEETING AT WIDNES. The annual vestry for Widnes was held last night at the overseers' office. Mr. J. Midwood presided, and there were eight other ratepayers present.—The Chairman said the overseers commenced the year with a balance in hand of £1,408 16.8 d., and the rate of 2s. in the £ pro- duced £12,438 3s. 4d. and bank interest £B7 ss. 4d., making a total income of £13,931 10s. 11d. The pay- ments included Union and County Calls, £9,158; Widnes School Board £3,800, and other charges £2lB 2s. 41., having a balance in hand of £755 7s. sd. The Chairman said he thought the balance was sufficiently large to justify them in issuing a 2s. rate for the ensuing year. The following gentlemen were nominated for the office of overseers :—Messrs. James White, J. Midwood (retiring overseers) Fred Neil, F. H. Pankhurst, W. Miller, Daniel Robinson, William Sadler, S. Owens, and Robert Booth.— On the proposition of Mr. J. E. Lee, ,seconded by Mr. Morrison, a vote of thanks was recorded to the retiring overseers and also to the assistant overseer (Mr. Goff) for their services during the past year, and the Chairman re- sponded. WELLINGTON COLLEGE, WELLINGTON, SHROPSHIRE. In the Cambridge University Locals the school has passed fourteen pupils, five of whom gained honours. In the College of Preceptors the sth, 6th, 7th, and 17th places in honours were won, and the school passed twice as many pupils in honours as any other school except one. This. it need hardly be said, is in the highest degree) creditable to the college. ARTIZANS AND SUNDAY OPENINGS OF MUSEUMS.

It is sometimes alleged that artizans do not care for the opening of museums and art galleries on Sundays. To put this queStion to the test the Executive of the National Sunday League have taken the • opinion of the journeymen hatters of London, by circulars issued to all the members of the society. The result of the voting is : For Sunday opening, 532; against, 52—in other words, ten to one in favour of the reform. EMIGRATINN.—Intending esnigratata to New Yolk. At a meeting of Liberals in Crewe on Wednesday night, a resolution of congratulation to the Irish members on the result of the Parnell/Commission and of confidence in the policy of the Opposition was unanimously adopted. The meeting also passed a resolution expressing satisfaction at the promise of Sir Richard Moon to guard in future against the possibility of intimidation of Liberals in the borough by the officials of the London and North-Western Railway Company. A RIVAL TO BRIDGET . KILDARE.

In our last issue we reported that the notorious Bridget Kildare, of St. Helens, had been convicted at the local Police Court, for tho 180th time. On Monday, at St. Helens Town Hall, Elizabeth Tither, another well known female, was placed in the dock for drunkenness. She informed the Bench that she went to the policetstation and asked to be locked up, but the officers would not take her into custody. It appeared she was disorderly °lnside the office and was then placed in the cells. It was her 144th appearance, and he was committed to prison for 28 days. -
GALA. AND SPORTS AT ST. HELENS.

----- A. gala and sports on a most extensive scale have been arranged to take place in a field at Denton's Green, St. Helens, during the Good Friday and Easter holidays. The field is within easy access of all parts of the town and district, and the venture should prove a great success. The attractions in- clude some of the best variety performers of the day, and among the " sights " will be performing lions, trained dogs' educated elephants, acrobats, trick cyclists, Herr Holtum, "the king of the can- non ball," roller skaters, braes bands, ikc. In addi- tion there will be all the paraphernalia of a regular fair.

A number of artists of repute have given their allegiance to the scheme. Among the names being those of Peter Ghent, James Towers, J. lil'Dougal, James Whaise, Isaac Cooke, C. L. Saunders. C. L. Kelly. Hampson Jones, James Barnes, Creswick Boydell, J. B. Mort, Harry lime, and Sage Seller. BICYCLES and TRICYCLF.S.—J. S. Garland. Warrington; Branch. Barlestown. - Advt. -,.

•. • „ FIRE AT nAINHILI, ASYLUM. About ten o'Clock, on Saturday night, a fire broke out at the farm buildings within the grounds of the Rainhill Asylum, but some distance from the Asy- lum buildings. As Mr. Blundell. the farm bailiff, and his family were retiring for :.,he night, a servant saw the reflection of fire throUgh her window and she immediately gave alarm. Mr. Blundell tele- phoned fo the Asylum office, and, in a short space of time a number of the attendants arrived with the apparatus. It was found that the Dutch barn, which contained several stacks of hay and straw, was on fire, and burning fiercely. Messengers were despatched to the Whiston Workhouse and St. Helens for the fire brigad..% and they attended with their steam engines. On their arrival the two bri- gades worked together to extinguish the fire which had obtained a good hold of the barn, and it was not till two and a half hours afterwards that they succeeded in doing so. The barn and its contents were destroyed and also an adjoining stack, and the damage will probably amount, to £250. It is not known how the fire originated. REGISTER GRATES.—J. S. Garland, 51, IS idge-street, War rington.—Advt.

A SHAKESPERIaN CATALOGUE. We have just received a copy of the new illustrated , catalogue of high-class watches, clocks, jewellery, I and electro-plate issued by Messrs. F. Meeks and Co., 100, Spencer-st., Birmingham. It is admirably prepared, and shows what a large-and excellent stock there is to select from. A special feature of the, catalogue is that each.page is headed with a text from Shakespere—most of them relating to "time,' the jewel" or "the watch." SERIAL'S ACCIDENT AT ST. HELENS. An alarming accident occurred at the " Bottom " glass works of Messrs.. Pilkington Bros., St. Helens, on Saturday afternoon, as a result of which con- siderable damage was done to the portion of the works known as the "No. 1 glass house. The furnace here is heated by gas, and, while the currents were being reversed, by some means a quantity of the gas exploded. One side of a chimney about 60 feet high was blown out, and a couple of hours later, while the remaining portion was being pulled down, it collapsed, with a loud crash. A lot of the bricks fell upon the glass house, the roof a which was destroyed. Some telegraph wires were torn down and other damage was done. Fortunately nob person was injured. DECISION. At a meeting of the Northwich Local Board, on Tuesday evening, under the presidency of Mr. J. Clough, the Clerk k Mr. Cowley) stated that he had had a communication from Professor Boyd Dawkins. in which he said that he had had an interview with Mr. William Topley, F.R.S., Geological Survey of Great Britain, as to his coming down to make an inspection of the district, and with a view of sup- porting Professor Dawkins in preparing a report. It was unanimonsly decided that Mr. Topley should be asked to meet Professor Dawkins, as it was considered that a report by him would prove invaluable with regard to the general question of subsidence.

RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS. A special meeting was held on Monthly night, Mr. J. W. Lightbara presiied, and there were pr-t- -sent Messrs. P. Speakman, 11. White, E. Imisan, S. Taylor, W. Hankinson, Fl. J. Grice, F. A. Lake (law clerk), E. Marshall (sec.), and Mr. Barker (surveyor).

div.head: ACCOUNTS.

It was resolved, on the motion of Mr. U. J. Grice, draw on the treasurer to pay accounts, to ckse the financial year. as follows :—General fund £333 7s. ; district fund £4O ; library fund £45 us. 10.1.

NUISANCES. It was unanimously resolved to serve notices upon several occupiers, to abate nuisances arising from over- crowding and from filthy condition of house. There was no other public business.

Buckley, P. Hall, .1. Whitlow, W. Pickering, Knowles, Brandreth, W. Whitlow, , Heywood, T. Hewitt, Bretherton, 11. Linaker (clerk). H. G. Linaker (deputy clerk), and J. THE SHIP CANAL AND SENVERAGE.—The Deputy Clerk I teported that a letter had been received from the Man- chester Ship Canal Company enclosing five plans, show- ing how it was intended to -deal with the various sewers and drains between Wilderspool and Frodsham.—Mr. Aaron moved thht the plans be referred to the Ship Canal Committee, and that the engineer, Mr. Wells, and the Clerk, be asked to confer with the committee on the subject.—Mr. Aaron observed that the MOST; strious part of the business was the syphon at Appleton, and the sewers at Frodsbam and Rock Savage.—" Che Clerk said the Local Government Board would give attention to any dispute that might take place, between the Authority and the Ship Canal Company.—Mr. Stokes seconded the motion,which was carried. THE COMPLAINT FROM HELSBY.—The Inspector of Nuisances reported thathe had inspected certain cottages situate at Helsby respecting whicii a complaint was read at the last meeting from Mr. Ffirish, but had found nothing stall to complain about. EXTENSION OF SEWER AT STOCKTON HEATIL—The In- pector submitted an estimate for a short extension of the man sewer at Stockton Heath and the consideration of the same was deferred to allow the Inspector to obtain further particulars in reference thereto.—The Inspector also reported that he considered it was quite necessary that an examination should be made of a length of sewer in Walton-road at a point lower down than where it is intended to connect the new sewer therewith, and it was decided that the Inspector confer with the Surveyor and obtain his views thereon, and, if requisite, instruct hiin to obtain an estimate for such examination. NUISANCES AT APPLETON. —Abated nuisances in this township were reported upon by the Inspector, and it was also reported that since last meeting Dr. Spears,from the Local Government Board, had visited the district in reference to the recent outbreak of typhoid fever. THE WHARF AT MOORE.-1 communication was read in reference to the depositing of manure upon the canal wharf at Moore, and the Inspector stated that he had communicated with the person interested in the matter : and he had no doubt but it would receive his prompt attention.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting was held on Tuesday. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner,ldessrs. Bretherton, Hewitt, W. Whitlow, Heywood, E. Aaron, J. Baguley, P. Hall, Knowles, Brandreth, J. Stokes, Pickering. Grice, S. Taylor, P. Speakman. J. W. Ragaley, D. 11. Jones, J. Jeffs, Jackson, J. Hall, Weir, H. Linker (clerk), and 11. G. Linaker (deputy clerk.)

OUR SOLDIER PkUPERS. The Deputy Clerk read a letter from the War Office in reply to a letter sent by the Guardians, in January last The letter stated that the question of inonthly pay- ment of soldiers' pensions had on several occasions been most mretully considered by thd present Secretary of State, and also by his predecessors, and that it had been decided that it would not be eenedient to adopt the course suggested, looking to the very great expense involved in the change and to the distress it would cause amongst pensioners at thf time of the alteration. It had been ascertained that the number of pensioners in workhouses or other- wise in receipt of relief from unions-did not exceed one per cent, on the whole number, and sei-ing that the pro- portion was so small, Mr. Secretary Stanhope could not consent to punish on their account., a body of more than 76,000 men, who had faithfully served the State in most cases for at least 21 years. He was quite willing to deal with cases in which it could be shown that the pensioners made habitual use of the unions and discharged themselves just before their pensions became due. In such cases special application should be made by the Guardians, direct to the War Office, and special orders would then be given re- garding the future mode of payment of such pensioners. With reference to the opinion expressed by the Guardians that in many cases the pension money exceeded the cost of maintenance and that the whole amount should be I paid to the Union during the chargeability of the pen-

sioner, he had to state that in view of all the circum- stances And more especially of the desirability of guarding against the permanent pauperism of pensioners as far as might be possible, Mr. Stanhope was unable to act upon the views of the Guardians in the matter. With regard to the Army reserve men, who belonged to a military force the members of which might, at any moment, be called upon to join the regular army, he had to acquaint the Board that it had always been held that the pay of an army reservp man could only be issued to the man himself and that the Secretary of State had no power to order that it should be stopped and handed over to the parochial authorities for the man's maintenance. USESSMENT COMMITTEE. The Assessment Committee recommended the re- appointment of Mr. H. Linaker as clerk to the Com- mittee, and on the proposition of Mr. Speakman, seconded by Mr. Aaron, the minute was confirmed. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE OFFICERS. The School Attendance Committee recommended that Mr. Riley and Mr. De Prez be re-appointed attendance officers for their respective districts, and that Mr. Ward be re-appointed fox the Weston district at an increase of salary of £5 per annum. It was also recommended that Mr. Tomkinson be re-appointed school attendance officer for Halton, in place of Mr. W. Howard, resigned.—ln reply to Mr. Brandreth the Clerk said the salaries of the attendance officers and clerk amounted to £125 per annurn.—Mr. Aaron said the cost was one-eighth of a penny in the £ and they had a better attendance than the school boards. He proposed the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Stokes seconded.—Carried.

div.p: PRESCOT BOARD_ OF GUARDIANS:

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians, was held at the Union Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday afternoon. The chair was occupied by tL Rev. Dean Finegan (chairman), theßev. S. A. K. Sylves- ter, Messrs. J. E. Chadwick, J. Griffiths, J. Mercer, J. A. Davies, J. Burchall, E. Syder, J. Peover, J. W. Wareing, J. Marsh W. Middlehurst, W. Lowe, J. Leatherbarrow, C. B. Johnson, W. THE COSY/CST COUNCIL AND THE GUARDIANS.—The Clerk read the minutes of a special meeting of the Guardians held on the 20th March to decide upon the steps to be taken to secure the payment to the Guardians of local grants pursuant to the Local Government Act, 1888. A letter was read from the Clerk to the Lancashire County Council intimating that the County Council were prepared to pay the Guardians' claims amounting to £4,01965. 4d. on an undertaking being given to repay such pro- portion of that sum as was claimed in respect of the period prior to the 31st. March, 1889, in the event of the High Court of Justice deciding that , County Councils were not liable to pay any contributions in substitution for annual local grants accrued prior to the 31st March, 1889. It was unanimously resolved that the untertaking referred to be given. It was further resolved that a similar undertaking te given to the Council of the County Borough of St. Helens and that the Clerk urge payment of the amount due (£2,944 15s. Bd.) before the expiration of the current half-year. —The minutes were passed and in reply to a question the Clerk stated that the respective sums mentioned had been paid. RELIEF.—Mr. Hale,- the Workhouse master,. reported there were 586 inmates of the House this week, the same number last week. 571 in the corresponding week last year; 59 vagrants had been relieved against 81 last year. THE FIRE AT RAINHILL.—The Workhouse Master re- ported that the Union Brigade were called to attend a fire at the R.iinhill Asylum farm buildings last Saturday night. The Clerk stated that the brigade did their duties extremely well and creditabty.—The Guardians considered the brigade deserved every congratulation, and accorded a hearty vote of thanks to them. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. —The School Atten- dance Committee submitted an estimate of the amount required in payment of expenses incurred by them dur- ing the quarter ending June next. The amount was £97 15s. THE WIDNES RELIEVING OFFICER.-1 later wa received from Mr. J seph Treaceya, relieving officer for the Widnes district, stating that he had mlt com- plied with the consolidated orders respecting the pro- duction of his completed accounts for the current half year, not from want of willingness or work on his part, but because it had been an impossibility. He respect- fully asked the Board to provide extra assistance in the work at Widnes. Several Guardians pointed out that relief business at Widnes had considerably increased during the last few months, and the letter was referred to the Widnes Relief Committee. THE CLERIeE SALAIIIES.—The Assessment Committee recommended that the Clerk be paid £l5O for his ser- vices as Clerk during the past year, and that he be further paid £lOO for extra duties outside the work attached to the office.—The recommendations were agreed to. _

RATEPAYERS' MEETING AT RUNCORN. The annual vestry . meeting of the township of Runcorn was held in Bethesda Schoolroom, on Thursday evening. Mr. H. Coleburn presided, and amongst those present were Messrs. W. Handley, W. Mellor, E. Imison, G. Moss. W. Hankinson, T. Cook, D. Bishrown' S. Yarwood, James Littler, E. Key, G. Torrie, John Littler, and W. Sutton (assistant ewer. seer).

div.head: BURIAL BOARD,
div.p: THE BURIAL BOARD,
On the proposition of Mr. W. Mellor, Mr. John Littler was appointed one of the auditors of the amounts. of the Burial Board; and on the proposal of Mr, D. Bisbrown,
Mr. Thomas Cook was appointed a second auditor. It was resolved that an adjourned meeting of ratepayers be held on the 24th April, to receive the report of the auditors.
NOMINATION OF OVERSEERS.

Mr. W. Handley nominated Mr. E. Imison and Mr. S. Taylor as overseers for the ensuing year. He said he knew something of the work, having been an overseer for 10 years, and he was glad to bear his testimony to the efficiency with which the present overseers performed their auties.—Mr. Mellor seconded the proposition, which was carried unanimously.— Mr. T. Ccok nominated Messrs. W. Mellor, Richard Morris, W. Hankinson, H. J. Grice, Jos. Pritchard, and W. H. Rogerson. The whole of the names will be submitted .to the magistrates for selection.—Mr. Imison (overseer) in acknowledging the vote, said any success which had attended the efforts of the overseers was mainly caused by the very brilliant example they had set before them, and by the efficient way in which the assistant overseer did his portion of the work. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: FINANCIAL.
div.p: FINANCIAL.

Mr. unison made a statement as to the financial position of the township. The overseers commenced the year with a balance of £1,039 13s. 3d.; the April rate of 10d. in the £ produced £2,225 16s. 11d.; and the October rate of ed. in the £ produced £1,352 Bs. 10d. The other receipts were, Ship Canal Company's deficiency account £l4 9s. 2d., bank interest £963. 2d., and voters' list, £1 10s.; total, £4,643 4s. 4d.—Mr. unison explained that the de- ficiency account was a new item, and had been caused through the construction of the Ship Canal. By Act of Parliament any property acquired during construction of works was free from rating, and did not appear in the rate book, but any deficiency which was caused in the " income of the poor rate must be made up. They had not to pay anything to the Commissioners' rate. The payments were as follows :—Justices' clerk's fees,£2 95.; rent, assistant overseer's salary, office expenses and sun- dries, £302 18s. 2d. ; registration of voters, £56 16s. 3d.• Runcorn Burial Board, £180; Runcorn School Board, £900; and Board of Guardians, £2,219. There was a balance in the bank of £982 Os. 11d. Mr. Imison gave " an explanation as to the necessity of this large balance.

div.head: CHARITIES OF RUNCORN.
div.p: THE CHARITIES OF RUNCORN.

Mr. W. Handley asked whether the trustees of the endowed and parochial charities of the township had sent to the overseers the accounts of these charities for 1889, and if so whether they were prepared to produce them.—Mr. Sutton replied that no accounts had been rendered to the vestry.—Mr. Handley then proposed that the overseers, on behalf of the vestry, request the trustees of the endowed or parochial charities for the township of Runcorn to furnish a copy of the accounts of such charities for the year ended December 31st, 1889, and that such copy of accounts be entered in the vestry minute book and produced at the adjourned meeting ot the vestry to be held on April 14th. Mr. Handley- said he did not make this proposal in a spirit of faction, or with any doubt as to the misappropriation of any charities, but so that there might be a statutory obligation com- plied with that ought to have been complied with for 30 years past. This was the only way in which a know- ledge of these charities could be kept in existEnce. He had been studying the question especially with refer- ence to the County of Cheshire, and he had been sur- prised at the large number of charities that had been lost in past years—entirely irrecoverable from the I loose way in which these public charities had been dealt with. The Charitable Trusts Act 1885 expressly pro- ' vided that these accounts othould be rendered to the vestry meeting of the parish. He had heard it said within the last few days that the vestry meeting 'of the parish was held at qv various churches in Easter week, but he pointed out that about ten years ago a certain act was put in force by the vestry, with the consent of the vicar and churchwardens, and by a special order of the Local Government Board, the vestry meeting was removed for ever from the Parish Church, and in future must be held in that room, which was hired for the purpose.—Mr. Key said there must be some minute to that effect, and Mr. Sutton produced the London Gazette for 1880, which contained an advertise- ment of the order referred to.—Mr. Mellor did not think the vicar would have any objection to produce the accounts of the charities to the vestry.—Mr. Hankinson asked if these accounts were submitted would the vestry have any control over the charities.—Mr. Sutton : No.— Mr. unison: The vestry would not be able to alter the disposition of a testator or anything of that kind.—Mr. Handley said it was simply that the accounts might be entered in the vestry minute book and their knowledge kept alive. He knew that the charities of Runcorn were all properly invested, and there was no question of mis- appropriation or misapplication.—At the request of Mr. Littler, Mr. Handley gave an interesting history of the Runcorn Charities.—After some discussion Mr. S. Yar- wood seconded the proposition,as he thought it was only just that they should know how these charities were dis- tributed.—The motion was carried unanimously, and the meeting was concluded with a vote of thanks to the Chairman.
UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES AT
RUNCORN.

The sixth and final lecture of the course on " Physiography " was held in Bethesda Lecture Hall. on Tuesday evening, when the subject of" Climates and vegetation "was dealt with by the gifted lec- turer, Mr. H. J. Mackinder in a highly instruc- tive manner. His explanations and descriptions were made more clear by a series of coloured views thrown on a screen by the oxy hydrogen lantern.—At the close of the lecture' Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys, the hon. sec. to the local Extension Lecture Committee, acknowledged in the name of those interested in the movement the service rendered by one er two gentlemen. First was their friend Mr. Horace Handley, who had so kindly aided the lecturer by superintending the oxy hydrogen lantern (hear, hear) and in future would be known as the honorary manipulator to the extension lectures. They were indebted to the Gas Company for having put in a special pipe to enable the illustrations to be given with due effect. (Hear, hear.) Mr. J. D. Jones, the librarian, although prevented from attending the lectures, had rendered valuable service, and had had charge of the University Travelling Library. He should be glad to receive all money for sold tickets as early as possible. The Students' Association would inset on Tuesday next as usual, and Mr. Annett would be present. He was desired to bring before their notice the University Extension Journal, which was of great interest and use to local centres. Mr. Humphreys further pointed out that there were a number of scholarships given in con- nection with the extension movement, and he should be glad to afford all information to students. The examin- ation onthis course was fixed for Wednesday, the 9th April, and he wished students who proposed sitting, to let him have their names and addresses, as early as possible, in order that he might make the necessary arrangements. In conclusion he announced that the, annual meeting of those interested locally in the exten- sion scheme would be held shortly, and it was wished that there should be as large an attendance as possible.— Mr. J. Pritchard proposed a cordial vote of thanks to Mr. Mackinder for the course of lectures he had given. They had been extremely interesting, and these who had attended, had greatly benefited, and their knowledge of the wide wide world was considerably increased. (Hear, hear.) They hoped to have the pleasure of again listening to Mr. Mackinder on some future occasion. (Applause.) Mr. J. Knowles seconded the motion, which was carried by acciammation. —Mr. Mackinder, in replying, said it had been a very great pleasure to him to be able to be it that region, and to be able to address four centres and one of 1 them Runcorn. At Altrincham he had what one might call a superior audience; at linutsford, a small audience almost entirely composed of ladies; at Warrington he. had been addressing an audience almost entirely composed of students, who were going to be elementary teachers ; and here at Runcorn, he had a most enthusiastic audience, and an audience which contained alarger proportion of gentlemen than he had seen at any of the other three towns. (Applause). This was an utterly different kind of audience to the others, and he thought they might claim that there the University Extension Scheme had scored an initial success this year. (Hear, hear.) They believed that to turn the. attention of the English public to things intellectual was to enrich Englishmen's lives. (Hear, hear.) He impressed upon them that they should make the University Extension centre permanent in Runcorn, that this success of the past year :hat these audiences with which they had honoured Mr. Shaw and himself, that this work which some of them had dontin written papers, that the further work which some of them were going to do in examination; that the reading they had had the opportunity of doing in the lending library sent down from the University * • that the reading which they all had the opportunity of doing in the public library; that the discussion which they had had an opportunity of carrying on in the Students' Asso- ciation ; that all this right act together in making such interests a real part ti their lives, in brightening, up some of the monotony which he knew too sadly accom- panied a great deal of their every day work ; and that therein they were making themselves better men and women and better English citizens. (Applause.) And possibly by so doing they might set at defiance, even the smoke which Widnes sent them (laughter). The lecturer referred to the summer meetings which annually held at Oxford, in connection with the Extension Scheme, when those who attended could see those wonderful buildings which had surrounded the greatest Englishmen in the students' days for many generation' past; to se l those splendid old libraries where knowledge was stored ; to see those Places where knowledge was to-day taught and to hear lectures on various subjects in which they might be interested. They wished Runcorn to take part in that movement, which in connection with Ox- ford alone, numbered 16,000 members. There were about 40,000 altcgether connected with the various extensions, and thousands of these gathered together every August at Oxford. Those who could not afford to go, coula, compete for scholarships, and he suggested that if there• were a surplus at Runcorn • to devote a portion to giv., jug a scholarship. Remember that depended not upon the Secretary, but upon those who attended the lectures. (Applause.)

FROM THE UNKNOWN WORLD,
THE ADVICE OF A VISION AND HOW IT
RESULTED.
(Leicester Midland Free Press.) TO TAX BDITOR. • 80. Oxendon-street, Leicester. 12th March, ,1890. •

Dear Sir,—The statement which I am sending you May appear strangeebut it is a true one, and I am ready at' all times to verify it, either by answering inquiries by letter, or by a personal interview. Some four years ago, while on a visit to my sister, I contracted a severe cold;which resulted in congestion of the lungs, accompanied by asthma. For a period of two years I experienced sufferings which I am unable to describe, being in constant pain, and never knowing what it was to get .a perfect night's res. I was unable to lie down at night, and had to take what little sleep I could get bolstered up in a chair, .oftela awaking with that terrible feeling of suffocation which all who are afflicted with this dread disease know so well. ' I was prevailed upon to seek medical advice, and called in a doctor of this town, who pronounced my case to be Chronic Asthma, and that he considered it to be incurable. Afterwards I called in another doctor, who prescribed medicine for me, and diagnosed my case as Incipient Consumption, which eventually would ter- minate fatally. I became a little better, which I attri- bute to the use of inhalation, but the relief was only temporary, and I gradually grew worse from day to day. I then had treatment from two other medical gentlemen of Leicester, who said that, in addition to Asthma, I also had Bronchitis, which could not be cured./ At this time I became so low that my friends despaired of my life, and prevailed on my going to Stockport, in order that I might have the advice and treatment of a 'epecialist. I was under treatment for a period of nine weeks. I then came home to Leicester, feeling ,better ! than when I went away, but in about five weeks 1 began I to feel that I was far from being on the read to recovery, I as one day, while sitting in my arm-chair, I felt a pecu- liar sense of oppression about the region of the heart, as if I were about to suffocate, being unable to breathe. I again went to Stockport, submitted to an operation; and again underwent muck snifering. I returned to Leicester, and continued the specialist's treatment, using his medicines, Sm., as directed, and at .the same time keeping him advised as to my conditioa. I found that the relief was only of a teraperary nature, and I had to return to Stockport. This time I did not experience the desired relief, as I had become so debili- tated from all I had gone through that my system seemed to be completely broken down.,. I went into the country with the hope that change of air would help me to recuperate, but in less than a week my husband was sent for to bring me home to die. It was at this time, while waiting for death, and sit- ting, withia the dark shadow, that the circumstances which led to my final recovery occurred. I had passed through a day of unrest, and could get no relief from my severe pains. , It was only With the great- est difficulty I could prevail on myself to remain in bed, as the thoughts of my little family being left bereaved nearly drove me wild. " _ . .

Towards night I became gradually more resigned to my fate, and gave my case in the ',Lord's hands, telling Him that as I had done all things tfrat_l knew in order to regain my health, and that as they had 'failed, would He point out the way to health if one remained, and if not would He break the tie gently and take me to Himself. • After this I fell asleep, and I seemed to realise that some one was speaking to me, as I heard a voice saying to me—" Take Warner's 'Safe' Cure." On till's I awoke, and I again heard the voice repeating the same words. , I said, "Warner's 'Safe' Cure ?" And again the voice rerieated the advice, adding, 4' Take it unsparingly and ungrudgingly." I would state that at this time I was wide awake, and seemed to see a shadow of some one in the room. I awoke.my husband and told him what I had seen and . heard, and he asked me if any person had previously advised me to use the medicine. I assured him I had not even heard of it. _ .

The next morning I procured a bottle as soon as possible, and took it as directed. I experienced relief from the very first dose, and continued taking it until I had used up two bottles. I was soon able to leave my bed and de my household work. My appetite gr ,dually grew better, and I could relish my fond, which before taking the Safe" Cure seemed hateful to me. I found that on retiring at night my rest was unbroken; my cough, which used to be so distressing, has left, me, and Ino longer feel that terrible sense of being suffocated, which had troubled me so long. My base is a wonderful one, and is the talk of all my friends who one and all wore sure that I should never be as well as I am to-day, and I cm thank God that I followed the advice given me from the unknown world to take Warner's t' Safe " Cure. _ _
Gratefully, (Signed) ELIZA CARTER.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
FRAUDULENT ENLISTMENT.

On Wednesday, at the Warrington Police Court, a well-built young fellow, named Wm. Yates; was charged with fraudulent enlistment. He enlisted in the King's (Liverpool) Regiment, at Warrington, and made a declaration to the effect that hehad never been discharged from the service. It transpired, however, that he had been dischared from the South Lancashire Regiment for felony. Prisoner, who told the magistrates that he re- enlisted because he was starving, was sent to prison for a month, with hard labour. A YOUNG WOMAN WHO IS DETERMINED TO DRINK. Sarah O'Brien, a Warrington young woman, has a ?enchant for prison. If she does like anything better, it is Warrington beer, and between the two her whole time seems tobe occupied. Her order of life apparently is to get drunk, go to jail, serve her time, get drunk again, and so on. Of the last twelvemonths, she has spent over six in prinon. In January she went to prison for a month. On the day of her release she was again arrested for drunkenness, and sent back for another month, and on Monday the Borough magistrates had again to deal with her on the'old charge. She returned to solitude and hard labour for yet another month.

div.head: WIFE DESERTION AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: WIFE DESERTION AT WARRINGTON.

Thomas Quinn, a labouring man, was brought before the Warrington magistrates on Monday on a charge of having left his wife to be maintained by the Union authorities. Mr. B. Shearer, who proved the case, said that prisoner's wife was admitted to the Workhouse on the 16th of July. A few days afterwards she left the institution, and is supposed to have joined her husband, who had gone out of the town. Prisoner came to Warring- ton on Saturday, and, a warrant being, in force, he was apprehended. As his wife had been chargeable for four days only, Mr. Shearer only asked for the payment of costs, and the amount due for maintenance, -Ss. in all. Prisoner promised to pay the amount on Saturday, and the case was adjourned for a week in order to allow him to do so.

div.head: OBSTRUCTION QUESTION
div.p: THE OBSTRUCTION QUESTION

On Monday, at the Warrington Police Court, John Gregg, furniture dealer, Winwick-st., was aummoned on a charge ef having caused an obstruction by placing his goods on the footpath outside his premises on the 15th inst. Evidence as given by Inspector Spinka to the effect that on the date mentioned he saw three round tables and one square table, tied to the front wall of the defendant's premises. They were not touching the ground, but a number of small articles were arranged on the cobble-stones. The Mayor said that it had been hoped that some arrangement would have been made between the Watch Committee and the Market Com- mittee respecting such obstructions. They would deal leniently with the present case, but in future the full penalty would be imposed. Defendant would have to pay the costs.
THE SHIP CANAL EMPLOYES AND THE MTIZZI IVO ORDER.

At Daresbury Sessions, on Tuesday, Thomas Phipps, employed on the Ship Canal, was char:zed with having on the Bth March. at Acton Grange, allowed two dogs to be at large in a public place in contravention of the- Muzzling of Dogs Order of 1889.—Mr. Jenkins; of Wart rington, appeared for the defence.—P.C. Barter said thae on Saturday morning, the Bth March, at nine o'clock, h t saw two dogs belonging to the defendant running abou near the huts at Acton Grange.—ln answer to Mr. Jenkins, the officer said he had been once told when going to the place in question that the road was a private one, and that he had no right there, hut he did not go away.—Sergeant Booth said he had been at the place several times, but had never been ordered away.—Mr. Jenkins said the fourth clailse of the Order Of 1889 read as foll?ws :—" Interpretation four. In this order public plate includes any street, highway, thoroughfare, public bridge, royal park, public park, garden, or pleasure ground, common, unenclosed land or other place to which the public have for the time being access." Clause Sread :=—"No dog shall be allowed to be in or on any public place unless such dog is muzzled with a muzzle so constructed as to render it impossible for such a dog while wearing the same to bite any petson or animal, but not so as to prevent such dog from breathing freely or lapping water." He submitted that the Ship Canal works was not such a place as was meant by the interpretation, clause. The public had no right of access to the Ship Canal works, indeed, they were treated as trespassers, and that•was borne out by the fact that notices were fixed up and down the works cautioning the public that their presence would be regarded as a trespass. If per- sons went on the works they did so at their own risk. Mr. Jenkins was proceeding with his contention, when the Chairman stopped him, and said the Bench were of opinion that the Ship Canal works was not a place within the meaning of the Act, and the case would, therefore, be dismissed .—Mr. Jenkins: This case has not been taken alp in an antagonistic spirit to the pqiliee. but Mr. Walker, for whom I appear, thought it his duty to contend for his private rights.—The Chairman: I am glad to hear you say so on behalf of the police, who amonly doing their aliet duty in bringing these cases before us.

div.head: EXECUTION IS LONDON.
div.p: EXECUTION IS LONDON.

John Neal, bricklayer, aged 64, was executed in New- gate Prison, on Wednesday morning, for the murder of his wife at Islington in January last. The murdered woman was very much younger than her husband, who was actuated by jealousy to commit the crime for which he suffered, owing to the provocation he had received, efforts were made to have the capital sentence com- muted, but without avail. The morning was dull and wet, nevertheless a crowd assembled and watched for the appearance of the black flag, which was hoisted at eight o'clock. The culprit walked firmly to the gallows. His last words were "I am sorry I committed the murder, but she was a bad wife to me." Death appeared to be instantaneous.

div.head: DOCK STRIKE AT LIVERPOOL.
div.p: THE DOCK STRIKE AT LIVERPOOL.

As the result of earnest advice given on Wednesday by Mr. Davitt to the Liverpool Dock Labourers, at a mass meeting held on the Pierhead, it is believed that the strike is at length almost as good as settled. Remind- ing his hearers that they had conceded the two conditions insisted on by the Employers' Association—namely, that the men themselves should negotiate with the employers, and that in the event of a settlement they would work peaceably with non-unionists—Mr. Davitt proposed that the meeting should appoint six of their own number to wait upon the employers. As the result of this proposal, a deputation of seven saw the Employers' Labour Associ- ation, and it was arranged that a further meeting for full deliberation should be held next day. At a special meeting of magistrates, held on Wednesday, it was de- I cided to retain the military for some time longer. On Thursday the deputation of Liverpool dock labourers, appointed on Wednesday, held an interview with the Employers' Labour Association, and subse- quently reported to a mass meeting that the masters insisted upon every man signing a guarantee to work peaceably and harmoniously with the imported men, that the masters should be at liberty to take back what- ever foremen they pleased, to take on the strike hands just as work could be found for them, and to exclude the quay porters from the benefit of the ss. per day offer. Mr. Bilkelly remarked that there was no concession which the employers were willing to grant. It was ulti- mately agreed that the deputation should once more try next day to arrange terms with the masters. Mr. M Hugh said he wished the deputation all success. Mr. Cunninghame Graham, M.P., in the course of some remarks, reproached the Employers' Labour Association with making their professions of willingness to negotiate a. sham. Notices to take a secret ballot of the dock labourers were on Thursday cancelled.

div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATT)RDAY, MARCH 29. 1890
THE BOAT RACE.

The University Boat Race took place on Wednesday afternoon, and was stubbornly contested throughout. Cambridge took the lead just after the start, but were soon passed by Oxford. At Hammersmith Bridge Cambridge recovered their supremacy ; but before Barnes Bridge was reached Oxford again wrested it from them and won by a length.
