div.head: RUG-BY.
div.p: RUG-BY.

WYCLIFFE V. ST. HELE-NVOIDMOYS.—This match was played on the ground of the former on Saturday, miserable weather. The h une team was fairly well . represented. Owing to the late arrival of the visitors, it was after four o'clock before the game was commenced. St. Helens winning the toss Wycliffe kicked off, the play for some time being of a give-and-take character, the home team having generally the best of matters. Tries were subsequently obtained by Beaman and " Smallman " (2, the place kicks in each instance failing.) These were the only major points obtained, the final score reading Wycliffe three tries and two minors St. Helens oneminor. I The home backs played a very effective and combined game, the passing being very commendable. Forward they still asserted their superiority, Lloyd, Hayes, , Burrows, and Johnson playing very well. The score does not indicate the true nature of the game, the visitors at times playing extremely well, their efforts to score being thwarted by the line defensive tactics of the home team.

WARRINGTON "A " V. BARROW "A"—This return fixture was decided at Warrington on Saturday, before a good assemblage of spectators, but the persistent rain which fell throughout the game militated greatly against correct passing. he Barrovians won the toss, and Thornley kicked off, but although no return was made, the visitors quickly took the ball to centre. Rowe soon made his presence felt by running round a pack to the quarter flag, and a kick of the visitors being charged Thornley almost scored. Immediately afterwards Antro- bus chucked smartly to Rowe, who as smartly dropped the ball over the bar. Barrow lost no time in re-starting, Barnes, however, running clean through the visiting backs. This was succeeded by some loose play, Thorn- ley, Russell, and Bate dribbling under the posts. A grand bit of passing by the home backs fairly roused the enthusiasm of the spectators, and again Rowe ran finely to the line, where Nevins, after a capital' bit of play, secured a try near the corner flag. The drop-out found Cox, Helsel!, and Fell rushing to the home quarters, and Haney fairly beating his opposing half, dribbled over the line, a minor resulting. A spell of exchange kicking ensued, Halsall, Cowen, and Huddart ultimately heading a fine dribble well into the home quarters. Very soon after this Eyres and Molyneaux. got away grandly along touch for half the length of the field, but the final pass was forward. Barrow responded by another really fine dribble to their opponents' 25. Then ensued a very fine display of passing. It was started by Antrobus, and the ball went through the hands of Barnes,,Eyres. Thornley, and Holmes, the latter winding up by beautifully dodg- ing Jones, and a further try was secured, which Barnes easily converted. After Barrow had relieved Eyres made a capital dribble, and then followed a bit of passing by Rowe, Holmes, and Molyneaux. A long kick by Waits was snapped up, by Webster, who after a very strong run got a good try, the visitors being obliged to concede a minor shortly after the drop out. Some give and take play next ensued, Barrow having considerably the worst of matters. Antrobus nextgot away with a tun and pass, and after Ashton had put in a short dribble, Nevins took the ball grandly and kicked well down the field, half-time arriving with Warrington 2-24t0 0-0-1. Restarting the homesters soon attacked which the visitors successfully cleared off, and then Nevins stopped a rush.. Hindle and Nevins put in capital runs for their respective sides, but ultimately Waits got finely away from a pack, and passed over to Babbs, who took play close to the War- rington line. Some very fine kicks between the oppos- ing backs ensued, and then Holmes led a long dribble to to the Barrow territory, and a tall kick from Webster brought severe pressure to bear on the visitors' defence, a minor being conceded shortly afterwards. This was succeeded by Barnes obtaining a couple of tries in quick succession from passes by Antrobus, one of which he converted. A spell of passing by Molyneaux, Antrobus, and Barnes resulted in the last-named securing another try, which he converted. Another good dribble by Eyres, Isherwood, and Thornley quickly took play to the Barrow quarters, where after some fine passing by Rowe, Antrolvs, Barnes and Webster, thelatter dropped a very smart goal. The same player soon obtained anothertry, and after some further passing amongst the home backs Bpeakman secured a try. Subsequently the visitors got into Warrington quarters, and aster a 'drop at goal by Haney, a try was secured by Halsall, Warrington win- ning easily by 5-5--3 to 0-1-1. After the game both , teams were hospitably entertained by Mr. Hatton, of the Seven Stars, where a most enjoyable evening was spent. The following were the teams :—Warrington BoscOw, back; Speakman, Barnes and Webster, three- quarters; Rowe and Antrobus, half-backs; Nevins, Molyneaux, Eyres, Ashton' Russell, Isherwood, Holmes, Thornley, and Bate, forwards. Barrow : Jones, back; Dickinson, Hindle, and Babbs, three-quarters •, Haney and , Waits, half backs ; Cox, Greaves, Fell, Halsall, Hudd art, Cowen, Field, Wolveridge, and Addison, forwards. WARRINGTON v. BARROW.

The Warrington team accomplished a smart perform- ance, on Saturday, when, in their return engagement with the Harrow Club, they succeeded in notching a victory by one goal, one try, to one goal, the last-named point of the Barrow team being the result of a penalty kick. When it is taken into account that this victory was gained without the aid of Barnes, Antrobus, Lawless, and Nevins, the victors is all the more credit- able, and praise is certainly due to those who performed in their stead for the able manner in which they acquit- ted themselves. The match, which was played at Cavendish Park, Barrow, was fought • under circum- stances which were disagreeable to the players awl spectators alike, rain falling during the whole of the game, whilst east wind blew across the ground. Barrow, with a full team started, and Jolley meeting the kick off, a well directed screw kick sent the oval well into the Barrow quarters. Free kicks to both sides were the opening items of the match, and neither side could claim an advantage, but from the first pack, formed at half-way, Mather slipped past the opposing halfbacks and eluding Harley, a capital run and pass took play to the Barrow line. For a considerable period the game raged here, a lucky kick by Leake eventually relieving, and Bate staying the further progress of the Barrovians with a capital save. A rush of the home forwards took play under the Warrington posts, but Jolley came away with a grand dribble to the half way flag, a free kick by the same player immediately after improving the " wirepullera' "position. At this point of the game, Davies was hurt, and although he continued the match he was of comparatively little use to his side. By the aid of good passing Barrow took play near the half way but a kick to Locket was mulled, and Handles rushing up took the oval, in grand style, and the issue was beyond doubt, for he sailed across the/line and placed the first try to the visitors' credit. Frank Turner took the place kick, the ball falling short by about a foot. Jolley and Evans by combined play again caused Barrow to defend, and another mistake by Lockett almost let the Warringtonians in. Evans made a gallant effort to get in, and although begot past Gregory, Wetherall pushed him in touch a yard from the line. The brothers Todd relieved with useful dribbles, but a penalty kicked to Warrington, and smart following up by Massey, again pressed the homestefs. Jolley crossed the line, but the point was disallowed, and Fair Turner also made several desperate efforts to get in, the whistle always stopping the Warringtonian's progress. Barrow rallied, and a pass from Bate being intercepted by Milner, a clear field, was presented the homsters, but Berry judged his man excellently, and half way saw his progress checked. Not to be denied, Barrow by strong rushes took play near the home lines, but the smart foot work and effective tackling of Warrington had its effect, and Bate with a neat dribble, coupled with a like movement by Frank Turner, W. Dillon, Povey, and Littlewood, changed the venue to the Barrow quarters. A good run by Milner relieved only for a moment, for Dillon, Davies, and Donohue headed a fine rush of Warrington to the Barrow line, Lockett serving smartly. The visiting skipper made an extra effort to score, and although he got to the line, some half dozen Barrovians managed at last tO bring him down. A. Hartley dribbled to the quarter flag, but his effort was neutralized by Bate passing to Evans, whose judicious kick sent the oval well inside the territory. A spell of even play followed here, aesniskick by Lockett causing a scrimmage near the home line. , Mather threw nicely to Massey. and before the homesters

were aware he had possession the line was crossed, and Frank Turner kicking a grand goal. Half time was called, with the score—Warrington, 1 goal, 1 try; Barrow, nil. Frank Turner restarted,,•ff side play ordering a scrimmage at centre. On the oack breaking - up W. Dillon, Frank Turner, Littlewood, and Handles headed a rush to the Barrow lines, and the plucky play of Milner and Lockett alone pre- vented them scoring. Passing was a difficulty, and how the players managed to keep erect in the. quagmire which the field of play undoubtedly was is a mystery. This they did admirably, and the game was above the ordinary, considering the circumstances under which it wasplayed. Bate and Massey:put in couple of grand kicks, neutralizing a long run by Milner hut Barrow by the aid of rushes and judicious kicking tolc the game near the visitors posts.. A. penalty kith was here awarded the homesters, from which:4llyr landed a neat goal. Towards the close of :the match Barrow made a .desperate effort toequalize,.andialthongh chances of scoring were missed by both sides no addition was made to the score, and after 80 minutes' play War-. rington asserted their superiority .for the second time this season by one goal, one try, to one goal.. That the best team won there is not the least doubt, for Warrington excelled in "every branch of the:game. To combination must the visitors owe their victory, the forwards especially so. The Warringtonians relied on dribbling rather than passing, and in this they sncceeded admirably. Berry played well in the fltst hale whilst of the three-quarters Jolley, who had the bulk of the work, played a grand game, And certainly outplayed Harley. Evans and Massey had not much work to do Mather created an impression with his play at half back, his effort in the first few minutes of the game at once stamping him as a useful player. Bates' play is well- known to readers of these columns, suffice it to say that it had in no way deteriorated. Fair TUrner and W. Dillon were the pick of a hard working set of for- . wards.

Teams :—Warrington : Berry, bac-k •, Massey, Jolley,. and Evans, three-quarters ; Mather and Bate, half backs : Fair Turner (captain), F. Turner, W. Dillon, E: =on, W. Randles, J. Donohue, T. Davies, W. Povey, and R. Littlewood. Barrow : Lockett, back ; Milner, Harley, and Gregory, three-quarters; Whitehead and Leake, half backs; R. Todd, J. Todd, Wetherall, A. Harley, Foley, Marshall, Simpson, Shaw, and Bolton,.forwards. Referee,.Mr. S. Troughton, Askam..

FOOTBALL—RUGBY. To-day's matches : Warrington v. St. Helens Recs.,. at St. Helens; Runcorn v. Broughton Rangers, at Run- corn; Widnes v. Stockport, at Stockport; St. Helens v. Lancaster, at Lancaster.

Only one of the four ties for the Yorkshire Cup, on Saturday, pioduced a severe struggle, Hunslet unexpectedly upsetting Halifax by two goals and four minors to two goals and two minors, or, according to the rules of the competition, by six major points to five. Huddersfield came out best, but they had the weakesVteam to face in Alverthorpe. Bradford and Wakefield Trinity had both, antagonists of better metal to deal with, and yet won with some- thing in hand. The semi-finals should prove highly in- teresting.

One of the mcst locally interesting matches of the West Lancashire League is to be played at Warrington, on Monday, between the home team and Walkden. The Walkden players have sprung into, prominence by the strong form they have i shown n these League matches, and only two or three weeks ago they very nearly broke the record of the invincible Wigan, team. Warrington, on the other hand, have not been seen at their best m the League matches, but in their ordiaaary fixtures they hwe lately reached high water mark, and with a strong team on their own ground, they are well-nigh unbeatable.

The St. Helens Recs. fairly beat Leigh on Saturday— both the flrst and" A "team matches resulting in vic- tories for the glass makers. For.some years past the Leigh organisation has been considered as keen rivals by the supporters of the St. Helens club and their "double defeat "last Saturday, was the occasion of much jubila- tion on the part of the Recs. club, and their enthusiastic adherents.

The champions of the West Lancashire League fairly took the starch out of the St.Efelens (Denton's Green) club. The score, however, is much heavier than the play war- ranted. The St. Helens men very often got near their opponents line, but their great fault was apparent to the spectators. They fail at critical moments to take advantage of the chances that are presented and the consequence is seen when the points at the end of the game come to be reckoned up.

div.head: .FOOTDALL-ASSOCIATTON.
div.p: .FOOTDALL-ASSOCIATTON.

By their failure in their final League engagement at West Bromwich, Everton have lost their chance of the championship. Had they won, it would have been necessary for the North End to beat Notts County on Thursday next, but no matter how the last-named game terminates, the Prestonians will again be champions, Everton could not come within three goals of the Albion, but 50111 e allowance must be made for the absent Latta, perhaps the cleverest forward in the team. He has not yet recovered from the injury sustained at Birmingham three weeks back, and his loss has been keenly felt.

The positions of nine of the League clubs are now settled. The first three places are filled by Lancashire clubs, whilst Accrington comes sixth: Bolton Wander- ers may rank eighth, and if they do there will only be one Lancashire team in the last four—Burnlev. It will thus be seen that the representatives of the County Palatine have come out of the tournament with much credit. The greatest advance has been that of Everton, who may not unlikely do even better next season, as they have an excellent team. Burnley have had an extraordinary time of it. After a most distressing run of ill-luck, they won four out of the last five games, finishing up with a draw at Bolton, although they were minus their centre forward for half the match. They have secured some first-class forwards, whilst their defence is both safe and sound.

The Committee of the County Antrim Football Associ- ation, met at Belfast on Wednesday night, and considered the circumstance's attending; the riot on the occasion of the final tie between Distillery and Linfi.ld on Saturday. in which one of the players had his le o broken. It was resolved to withold the County Antrim Shield and medals this Year, and one of the Distillery team was sus- pended.

div.head: CYCLING.
div.p: CYCLING.

On Good Friday the St. Hele'ns cyclists will commence operations for the season by visiting Warrington and floc. Green. They will partake of dinner and tea at the Norton Arms, Warrington, as in former years. It is interesting to note that the St. Helens Cyclists' Club still enjoys the popularity and success that have attended its movements for the past fourteen years.

div.head: WONDERITI, AIR SHIP.
div.p: A WONDERITI, AIR SHIP.

According to the London edition of the " New York' Herald," there is in construction in the neighbourhood of, London an air-ship or balloon, the inventor of whick chums that it will be perfectly manageable, and capable of doing 120 to 150 miles an hour in calm weather, and not less than eighty miles an hour against the stiffest headwind, with a crew of several men on board—and enough dynamite to wreck any town or fortress on which it may be dropped.

div.head: TAB WIGAN MURDER:
div.p: TAB WIGAN MURDER:

William and Ann Dickinson were again brought before. the Wigan -county magistrates on Tuesday morning, charged with murdering Hannah Lydia Birchall, at bee, on the sth inst. Mr. Lees appeared for the male pris- oner, and Mr. Wilson for the female. Mr. Ellis prose- cuted on behalf of the Treasury, and &tailed the pro- ceedings leading up to the disappearance of the child and the subsequent discovery of the body in an old coalpit shaft. He should ask the Bench to committ both pris- oners for trial.
THE QUEEN'S DEPARTURE FOR THE

CONTINENT. The Queen, with Princess Beatrice, Prince Henry of Battenberg, and suite sailed from Portsmouth on Tues- day morning on board the Royal yacht Victoria and Albert for Cherbourg, whence her Majesty and Royal party will proceed to Aix-les-Bains. A Reuter's telegram from Cherbourg states that the Royal, yacht arrived in the harbour there at three o'clock on Tuesday afternoon. Immediately on disembarking, the Royal party entered a train which was lighted with electric light, and left on their way to Aix-les-Bains. The route from the arsenal to the railway station was lined with troops.

div.head: TilE SALFORD- SCANDALS.
div.p: TilE SALFORD- SCANDALS.
ACTION 'AGAINST MR. ELLIS LEVER.

The action by the Mayor and otTrWrallcTM of 'Salford against Mr. Ellis Lever for the recovery of moneys amounting to £2.329 alleged to have been paid by Mt. Lever in the shape of bribes to Samuel Hunter, the late gas manager of the Corporation, was tried on Tuesday in the Nisi Prins Court at the Leeds Assizes, before M. Justice Day and a special jury. Hunter and other wit-. nesses were called to prove that bribes to the amount stated had been paid by Lever. No witnesses werecalled for the defence, and in consequence of ill-health the de— fendant was unable to be present in court. In his answer to interrogatories, which were read by plaintiffs' coun- sel, he stated that he declined to answer the interroga- tory as to whether he had given bribes to Hunter, as he had been advised that he was under }lo obligation to de so, and if he did so his answer might tend to incrimin- ate himself. The only question was as to whether or not the right of the plaintiffs to recover from Mr. Lever was barred by the much talked of " compact " entered into between Hunter and the Corporation. On this point of law his Lordship decided against the defen- dant, and the jury returned a verdict for the plaintiffs for the full amount claimed. His Lordship consented 'to• stay execution for a few days.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND)
div.p: STATE OF IRELAND)
SHOCKING ASSAULT BY A WIFE.

At Cork, a married woman named iia-m" Mon+, on waking from a drunken sleep, accused her husband'of stealing half a sovereign from her pocket. The husband denied the accusation, whereuprtn the woman hurled a cup at him. It broke on his neck, and cut an artery, causinr, the man to nearly bleed to death.. Re isin, the hospital in a weak state. The wife is in custody. DISORDERLY MEDICAL .STUDENTS.

On Saturday, in Dublin, a great sensation was caused by about 150 medical and other students marching in procession through the principal streets in imitation of the builders' labourers now on strike in the city. They carried a banner and broomstick, and became so disor- derly that the police arrested a number of them. The prisoners were at once taken to .the police court and heavily fined. ALLEGED MURDER IN TIPPERARY".

A man named Grant was charged before the magis- trates at Thurles, county Tipperary, on Tuesday-, with causing the death of Mr. Burke, road contractor, who succumbed on the 17th inst. to injhries to the head, in- flicted thve days previously. Illafeelitig arisihg out of business rivalries existed between the two men, but they drove home together in the same cart with, another man from \Nenagh fair. On the way Grant and Burke alighted, and the former attacked the latter with a shovel. Burke on his deathbed identified Grant as the man who attacked him, and he was committed for trial on the capital charge.

div.head: CREWE MURDER.
div.p: THE CREWE MURDER.
PETITIONS_ FOR A. REPRIEVE,

The petition praying for the commutation of the death sentence upon Richard and George Davies is being exten- sively signed in Crewe and the neighbourhood. Mr. Pedley, prisoners' solicitor; has forwarded one to the House of Commons Library forthcesignature of members of Parliament. The petition says the evidence tends to show, and the memorialists believe, that the prisoners had been driven to desperation by the almost incredible cruelty and brutality to which during a long series of years, the deceased mamhad• subjected their mother and the rest of the family. The memorialists further state that while there is no excuse for the commission of the crime, the extreme youth of the prisoners, their up- bringing, and the terrible provocation which had been given should rightly be considend in deciding upon their punishment. The condemned youths are stated to be heartbroken on account of their awful position. They attend diligently to the ministrations of the chaplain. On Saturday Mr. Pedley, solicitor for the brothers Davies,condemned toAeath for the murder of their father, said he had received a large number of applications for petitions in favour of commutation of sentence, and he believes the jury's• recommendation, emphasized by public opinion, will indUce the Home Secretary to extend the cleMency of the Crown. Thir: brother of the con- demned lads states that the other members of the family refused to believe in their guilt until the prisoners had cmfessed.

- Since their committal the prisoners buoyed themselves up with the hope that they iniwlit .et off. They did not appear to fully realize the enormity of their crime until I after the death sentence had been bassed upon them. Then, unable to restrain their feelings longer, they both., sobbed piteously, wrung their hands, and gave way to uncontrollable grief. After the sentence both were kept' in, one cell, and when visited were too much overcome to steak. The mother of the prisoners, who gave evidence, against them, was much prostrated on hearing that Ler sons had been sentenced to death. Richard (the brother says) was kindly, affectionate, tender-hearted and obe- I dient, but George was sullen and morose, and sometimes exceedingly strange in manner. DATE OF EXECUTION FIXED. The _High Sheriff of Cheshire (Mr. Jardine) has:fiXed Tuesday, the Bth April, for the execution at Knutsford Gaol of Richard and George Davies, for • the murder of their father at Crewe.

Mr. Pedley, solicitor, has received a letter fnotri, the Home Secretary, asking for a plain statetnent a the grounds on which the plea for mercy on behalf a the condemned lads Richard and George Davies iS.tased, promising to give it his most careful consideratioa. It is not expected that the decision of the Home Seeretaay will be madeknown until the middle of next week..

div.head: IMPROVEMENT BILL.
div.p: IMPROVEMENT BILL.

Sir,—Like many other ratepayers, I feel somewhat undecided as to the way in which I shall vote. Aepord- ing to the voting paper, I am asked whether I am in favour of taking over the Water Works, Extension of the Borough, to make better provision for the health, local government and improvement of the Borough. &e. While agreeing with the latter provisions,which,as far as I can hear, it is admitted would greatly benefit the town, still I am not in favour of the Water Works purchase at the price ; but, if I disagree with this and vote against it I veto the whole bill. This I think most unreasonable. The opposition seems to be to the clause relating to the Water Works purchase, and I think that this and this alone is what we should have been asked to vote upon. If this had been the case and the voting had been against it, the other portion of the Bill could have proceeded, and the money already expended would not have been a dead loss. I should not like to vote against the exten- sion and improvement, and I should not care to vote for the Water Works purchase. What am Ito do? QUERY. The law requires, we believe, that the vote shall be for or against the Bill as a whole. It is for our Corres- pondent to decide for himself whether his opposition to the proposal to negotiate for the purchase of the Water Works is stronger than his liking for the rest of • the Bill.—En. Ex.

- GROSS MISSTATEMENTS.—A CORRECTION. Sir,—l have forwarded the annexed letter to the Editor of the "Journal of Gas Lighting, Water Supply, &c.," and, as the paragraph to which it refers has been quoted by one of your local contemporaries, I shall esteem it a favour if you will publish my comments upon it.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, Warrington, 25th March, 1890.

div.head: J. L. TUNSTALL.
div.p: J. L. TUNSTALL.

- Sir,—My attention has been called to a somewhat remarkable paragraph which appeared in your issue of the 18th inst., with reference to the proposed purchase by the Warrington Corporation of the undertaking of the Warrington Water Works Company. The point which more immediately concerns me is the allegation which you say is made that a sum amounting to nearly £3,000 has been entirely omitted from the calculations, and, as I am responsible for the calculations to which you probably refer, I shall be glad if you will give me the oppor- tunity of saying that there is absolutely no founda- tion for the statement, and that the paragraph in question gives, so far as I know, the first intimation of any such statement. I forward you herewith a copy of a report upon the financial aspect of the matter which I made to the General Purposes 'Committee of the Corporation, and a copy of the last statement of accounts of the Water Company, and shall be much indebted to the writer of the paragraph if he will point out the alleged discrepancy. I cannot allow /his opportunity to pass without some further comment. The statement that the Company have agreed to accept, and the Corporation to pay, a sum of £270,000 is not true. The Company could not, under any circumstances, agree to sell witheut submitting the terms to its stock and share holders. The question has not been con- sidered by the latter, and there is not even a conditional acceptance of the terms by the directors, though there are good reasons for believing that they would be agreed to. All that the Corporation have done is to make an offer of certain terms which are to become bind- ing on their part if the ratepayers and Parliament approve, and if ;3atiefactory reports be made by competent persons to be appointed to inspect the works and accounts. The remark that "it is clear that the effect of the purchase will be to add a ' sum which may be Bd. and is certain to be at least 30. in the pound to the existinz local rates "is as fallacious as the statements already referred to. The resignation of the Town Clerk, whose ability no one will call in question, is not likely, as regards this matter, to prove the great misfortune you appear to anticipate. The reverse, rather, is the case, inasmuch as through his instrumen- tality an offer has been made to the Corporation by the petitioners against the Bill whom he represents to pay the Corporation a suvn equivalent to the probable increase in the rates, and I may add that the Corporation have in their newly-appointed Town Clerk, a gentleman who is quite competent to deal with the Bill and who has been familiar with it from the first. This is intended as a refutation of some only of the assertions made, and I do not propose to waste your valuable space by a reference to the absurd insinuation of mystery, and goodness knows what beside, with which the writer has sought to give force to his ill-con- ceived effusion. Very little reflection upon the true position of affairs will probably lead you to the conclu- sion that we are not in the habit of acting, even in War- rington, quite so idiotically as some people would lead you to imagine.-4 am, sir, your obedient servant. J. L. TUNSTALL.

div.head: WATER CHARGES :-LIVERPOOL VERSUS WARRINGTON.
div.p: WATER CHARGES :-LIVERPOOL VERSUS WARRINGTON.
Sir,—ln the Supplement to your paper of Marc t 22nd, you make the following comments on a letter of mine dated March 11th, 1890 :
"REASONABLE TERMS.

It is, of course, a legitimate matter for discussion whether the Water Works Company are at the present time supplying the people of Warrington with water upon reasonable terms.' Mr. T. Greaves, who has twice written i,s on the subject of the purchase of the water undertaking, and who has a strong objection to the pur- thase, contends that the terms are not reasonable; but as to this it should be pointed out that the Water Works Company are limited as to their charge by an Act of Parliament. They are charging the maximum rate, and they are entitled to do so. Mr. Greaves produces a startling contrast by stating that the charge for water in Liverpool 'is at the rate of 6d. in the £on the nett assessment for an abundant supply suitable for any purpose. In Warrington the Charge is is. 2td. for domestic purposes only. We unfor- tunate consumers pay 81d. in the £ in excess of Liver- pool.' Such a difference is certainly extraordinary; but as a matter of fact there is no such difference in price, for it happens that Mr. Greaves has omitted to state, inadvertently of course, that at Liverpool, in addition to the rate of 6d in the £ on the nett assessment, there is a water rate to be paid of 6d. in the L. It will be seen, therefore, that the difference really is one of one shilling in the £ in Liverpool as against is. 21d. in Warrington, a differehce which cannot be said to be extraordinary." In reply to these comments permit me to make a few observations. You assert as a fact that the difference between the charge to the Warrington water consumer, is only 2fd. more"than that charged to the Liverpool con- sumer. In this you are in error. In order to be strictly accurate, I called at the Liverpool Municipal Offices and I find that they have this year increased the charge to the water consumer from the 6d. in the L quoted by me to Thd., so that my figures were correct with the excep- tion of the increased levy of 1/d. this year. With regard to the 6d. rate mentioned by you, it would have been incorrect for me. in making a comparison between the cost of water to the consumer in Warrington and the consumer in Liverpool, to have added the 6d. rate, which is a rate not charged to water consumers as consumers, but a rate levied on the owners of property, and occupiers, and the payment of which rate is equally divided between theiti. Had the Warrington Corporation made provision in their bill to enable them to levy a similar rate to this, the whole burden of the purchase of the Water Works would not have been thrown upon the - water consumers alone : but owners of property and the occupiers of large works, manufactories, &c., wile do not -use the Company's water,would contribute their share to -the cost of what is for the benefit of the town at large, themselves included .--SincerelY yours, THOMAS GREAVES. The Tower, Warrington, March 27th, 1890.

'The whole difference between us and Mr. Greaves is one of mode of payment. In Warrington the consumer pays is. 216. in the £ in one sum ; in Liverpool he pays Md. as consumer and a 6d. rate as a ratepayer: showing a difference in this respect of nine-tenths of a penny only in favour of Liverpool. We grant that something may be urged in favour of beginning, as in
Liverpool, with a special levy of a fixed sum, and should be glad to hear something more as to this phase of the question.—ED.
THE CORPORATION BILL, AND THE QUALITY

div.head: OF WATER.
div.p: OF WATER.

Sir,—My proposal that the Winwick water should be analysed appears to have met with general favour. If the water is bad, as alleged by Mr. .Diggle and others, then the fact had better be recognised, so that it may have due-weight when actual negotiations for the pur- chase commence. If, on the other hand, the water is not below the average of ordinary drinking waters, then let the Corporation and the Water Company have the benefit of the truth. Before adding a word or two on the prime necessities of a domestic water, I wish, with I your permission, to make a brief reference to the facts and opinions of Mr. Diggle. Mr. Diggle is no doubt an authority on dyeing—especi- ally blue dyeing. Now blue dyeing requires a large amount of lime to set the vats. How then can Mr. Diggle have been inconvenienced by a calcareous water? The same reasoning applies to blacks, oranges, ambers, &c., all of which require the use of time. The presence of iron in the water is far more dangerous than lime in the operations of the dye-house. Up tea certain point, a calcareous water is distinctly beneficial. To contain no lime is almost as objectionable as to con- tain too much. While conducting a turkey red process in a town where the water was very pure, I had to see that a small quantity was put into the dyeing water. The colour would have been dull and dead unless this had been done. "But," objects Mr. Diggle, "if you have a pure water you can put the lime in, while you can't well take it out of a bad water." Quite true. But this would amount to the admission that the presence of a little lime is not so objectionable as we have been led to believe. Will he admit this? _ _

Now as to the specimens of boiler scale in the posses- sion of Mr. Diggle. Are they really the products of Winwick water? The boilers of the firm alluded to are supplied from a well on the premises, and the water con- tains a large amount of solids. If the specimens are from the boilers of Armitage and Rigby, Limited, then Mr. Diggle is misleading the public on this matter. Scales and encrustation, the products of a private well supply, throw no light cn the quality of the Winwick water. Perhaps Mr. Diggle will explain? Now we are to have an analysis, it is to be hoped this question will be settled once for all. We cannot mend the water, but we may know what we are buying. The two essentials of a good drinking water are : Freedom from organic matter. Comparative absence of earthy and saline matter. The organic matter is related to the health of the community; the mineral solids to its convenience. The presence of organic matter, which is the product of decaying vegetable and animal life, is highly dan- gerous; and a water containing more than two or three grains per gallon would be unsuitable for drinking pur- poses. As to the inorganic impurities, perhaps the most annoying constituent to the householder would be magnesia. It decomposes soap more readily than lime. Pure water is insipid ; few would like to use it regularly; but water containing lime is bright, sparkling and pleas- ant to the taste. The total number of grains of solid matter per gallon varies considerably. Compare the following : Grains per gal Loka River (Sweden) .05 Bala Lake Thirlmere The Danube 917 Three London Water Co's. average 24.00 _ . . .

In conclusion, it is to be expected thatheAnalyst will, after giving the result of the ordinary chemical examin- ation of the water, estimate the degrees of hardness by means of the soap-test. This is the practical test and the one which will commend itself most to the under- standing of the ratepayers. As to the Bill itself, I think it would be a pity for the ratepayers to reject it. But I cannot help concluding that it would have been a sounder, a wiser, policy if the quality of the water, the condition of the plant, and other matters, had been gone into by competent author- ities before the assent of the ratepayers was asked. Yours truly,
IV: :1. BUTLER.
Latchford.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO A RUNCORN WORKS MANAGER.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO A RUNCORN WORKS MANAGER.

An interesting ceremony took place at the works of Messrs. Wigg Bros. and Steele, Old Quay, hun- corn, on Wednesday evening. About live o'clock the workmen gathered in the joiner's shop, where a platform had been constructed, for the purpose of bidding farewell to the manager, Mr. William Towns, who has been connected with the works for about ten years. Mr. Turnbull took the chair and delivered a brief though appropriate address, and afterwards Mr. Fred Normanon behalf of the men, presented Mr. Towns with a solid silver tea and coffee service and a silver watch, supplied by Mr. Joseph Pritchard, of Bridge-st. The watch bore the following inscription :—" Presented with silver tea and coffee service to Mr. William Towns by the employes of Old Quay Copper and Alkali Works, as a token of their esteem, and with their best wishes for his future welfare. Runcorn March 28th, 1890." Mr. Towns suitably acknowledged the gift, and described the progress which the works had made during the time he had held the position of manager. Several of the workmen also made speeches, in which they referred to Mr. Towns in terms of praise. At the conclusion of the proceedings, hearty cheers were given for Mr. Towns, and "For he is a jolly good fellow" was lustily sung forth. Mr. Towns has accepted the position of man— ager to Messrs. Hutchinson and Co., chemical manufac- turers, Widnes.
FOOTBALL.

RUNCORN V. LIVERPOOL OLD BOYS " A " TEAMS.— Played at Fairfield on Saturday in rough wet weather; The visitors scored an easy victory by 1 goal, 5 tries, 1 minor; to Old Boys 1 try, 1 minor. VVIDNES ST. MARY'S V. ars L.A.V.—These teams met for the first time this season at Wavertree on Saturday. Widnes held the upper hand throughout and ran out the winners by 2 goals, 2 tries, and 9 minors to nil.

FRODSIaII v. FIRS.—FI:OgiShaM met the Firs team on Saturday, on thezround of the former, in wet weather, and a capital garhe resulted. Frodsham scored three goals, four tries, and two minors, to the Firs nil. The tries were scored by Fred Darlington (2), W. Tudor (2), Ilenshaw, Rogers, and J. A, Tudor. RUNCORN V. LIVERPOOL OLD BOTS.—The return match between these teams was played at Runcorn, on Satur- day, when there was a large number of spectators lining the enclosure. The ball was set in motion by Faulkner, and play was very quick. Legge having kicked into touch from the line-out, Wood passed to Atkinson, who ran well in at the corner flag. The attempt at goal, however, failed. Subsequently the game was warmly contested, and Riley, Crompton, and Davies resorted to a passing game, and the latter got over after one of his runs. The goal failed. Then the Liverpudlians carried the ball to the home line, but Runcorn broke away, and the visitorswere considetably pressed. Crompton essayed a run, and Ray, in the nick of time, saved. BroulY, when the home forwards got in the visitors' quarters, got over, but again the goal failed. At half-time the score was—Runcorn, 2 tries, 1 minor ; Old Boys, 1 try. After the usual interval, Gould re-started, and the ball was rushed up to the visitors' line, whore some fine play was observed, and Legge, who received a pass from Atkinson, got over, but the place kick failed. Runcorn, however, did not seem to play with that dash and spirit which has been noticeable of late, but one thing may be stated that they were without the services of one or two of their prominent players. The score at the conclusion of the game was—Runcorn, 2 tries, 3 minors; Old Boys, 2 tries.

WIDNES E. OLDHAM. —This match was played at Widnes, on Saturday, before a large number of specta- tors. Smith started the ball for the home team, and after some long kicking, the ball settled in the home quarter. McGurl relieved by a pass to Brennan, who, after making a splendid run, passed to Peters, who was not collared until he was in the act of crossing the visi- tors' line. Clarke and Hartles were again conspicuous in holding the position the local team had gained, and the pressure was kept up by some good passing by Stubbs and Laws, until Farrell kicked over the line, where it touched down. Stabbs and Laws dribbled well after re- starting, and subsequently Gordon got over, registering the first major point. The place kick, which was a very difficult one, was taken by Brennan and proved success- ful. From the drop out the visitors invaded the home quarters, but Brennan received a pass from Farrell and made a splendid run from one end of the field to the I other, but was thrown in touch. Clarke next got pos- session, and secured a try, but the place kick failed. At half-time the score was—Widnes one goal, :one try, and one minor, to Oldham nil. On changing ends the visi- tors started the ball, and immediatel pressed, a try being subsequently scored by them. No goal, however, re- sulted. Some penalty kicks having been exchanged, 1 Peters received a pass from Brennan, whl after putting in his kick followed up, and having got possession again baffled his opponents by his dodgy play, and crossed the line amidst enthusiastic cheers. The place kick again proved fruitless. Clarke and Peters were again conspi- cuous with some good running and tackling. Hurst and Nolan being respectively caught by them after a sprint half the length of the field. The ball was then carried again to the visitors' line, where Farrell threw to Bren- nan and then to Laws, the latter getting a try ; but some oversight on the part of the referee resulted in the ball being called back, Hurst again got away and scored a try just before the call of "No time." The place kick fell short. The game ended in a victory for Widnes by one goal, two tries, and one minor, to Oldham two tries. Teams :—Widnes: Hartles, buck; Clarke, Brennan, and Peters, three-quarter backs; Farrell and McGurl, half backs; Stubbs, Laws, Holt, Gandy, Pearson, Farmer, Smith, Gordon, and Whelan, forwards. Oldham : Ben- nett, back; Pennington, Hurst, and Macdonald, three- quarter backs ; Nolan and Thames, half backs; Court, Blomlev, Ingram, Pendlebury, Armstrong, Giles, Drons- field, Darlington, and T. Holden, forwards. Referee, Mr. Hunter, Manchester Rangers.

div.head: RUNCORN TONIC SOL-FA CHOIR CONCkIIT.
div.p: RUNCORN TONIC SOL-FA CHOIR CONCkIIT.

- -- The third concert of the season was given in Runcorn Public Hall, on Monday evening, and, although the audience was not of large proportions, the concert was a. success financially, and was highly enjoyed musically. Thefirst part of the pro- gramme consisted of Dr. Stainer's sacred cantata "The Daughter of Jairus," which has been selected by the Association of Tonic Sol-Fa Choirs for perform- ance at the Crystal Palace, in June. The choir dis- played their customary effectiveness and tunefulness in the choruses, and reflected great credit upon Mr. John Holford, the able and painstakingconductor. The prin- cipals were Soprano, Miss Ada Lee; tenor, Mr. H. Daniels; and bass, Mr. J. Peers, all of Manchester, and the various solos received full justice at their hands; the music being in harmony with the sad and pathetic story of the cantata. The second part con- sisted of sacred items. The choirrendered "There is a green hill far away," and 'A# Hymn of the Homeland" in capital style. Miss Lee's best effort was "From mighty kings," for which she received an enthusiastic encore, and in response she gave a charming rendering of "The Children's Home." Mr. Daniels was heard to advantage in the recitative" Ye people rend your hearts," and aria "If with afi your hearts" from Mendelssohn's "Elijah," and he was loudly applauded. "Honour and Arms," from Handel's Samson, was given by Mr J. Peers with considerable power and expression, and his interpretation of the song "Eternal Rest" was much enjoyed. The concert was brought to a conclu- sion by " Agnus Dei," in which the solos were ably taken by Miss Lee and Mr. Daniels. Mrs. W. R. Kay fulfilled the duties of accompanist, and Master B. Musgrove had charge of the harmonium. In bidding Mr. Holford and his choir " good-bye " for another season, it is with the hope that they will enter upon another year with renewed vigour, and that they will receive a greater measure of that pnblic patronage which they so we" deserve.

div.head: MELANCHOLY FATALITY AT WES2ON
div.p: MELANCHOLY FATALITY AT WES2ON
POINT.
THE DEATH TRAP AGAIN: TWO PERSONS DROWNED.

To the already long list of drowning accidents on the Runcorn and Weston Canal, another sad record was added on Saturday night. The victims on this occasion were William and Elizabeth Dunning, an elderly couple, aged respectively 63 and 69 years,who lived on Weston Point. On Saturday night they were "marketing" in Runcorn, and between eight and nine were seen returning home along the towing path of the canal, the only direct means of com- munication between the two places. They were passed by several friends on the road, and a young man named White kindly relieved Mrs. Dunning of a besket she was carrying. The aged couplenever reached West- on Point, and next morning a boy saw their de: d bodies floatingln the canal near the Salt works Bridge, a dan- gerous epot where many lives had been previously lost. The Coroner, Mr. J. E. Worsley, held an inquest on the bodies at the Dock Hotel, on Tuesdaf afternoon. Mr. T. Simister was present on _behalf of the Ship Canal Co., and Inspector Bowyer represented the police.—Sarah Antrobus, wife of John Antrobus, labourer, and daughter of the deceased, said her parents had lived at Weston Point 23 years. She last saw them alive about 8 o'clock on Saturday night, in Runcorn. They were on their way home along the towing path of the careal,.which was the usual way to Weston Point. It was a dark and wet night. By the Coroner: She did not know her parents had not come home until her brother went to the house. She thought they had gone with Mrs. Abrams,. who had fetched her mother to go to Runcorn.—After witness had retired, the Coronee asked if the deceased were a united family.—Mr. Rozenberg (foreman of the jury) replied so far as he knew .—Agnes Abrams, wife of Enoch Abrams, Batman, Weston Pbint, said she saw the deceased at the "Big Office" about nine o'clock. They said they were coming home, and Mrs. Abrams told her to go on and they would overtake her. They were quite sober. Shed had no idea how they had fallen its unless the " old woman" had missed her footing and fallen into the canal, and the "old man" had fallen in by trying to save her. They had both walked along the canal bank scores of times. The night was dark and wet. She did not hear of their death until Sunday morning.—Joseph White, Lunt's Row, dock labourer, said on Saturday night he called in the Duke of Wellington Hotel,. Percivars-lane„ and had a glass of beer. The deceased' were there. They said they were going home, and he accompanied them as far as the Duke's dices, when Mr. Dunning requested him to go ahead and wait for him at Mr. Fitton's. Ho did so and carried Mrs. Dunning's basket, which was rather heavy. He waited from 25 past nine until a few minutes after ten, when he left the basket at Mrs. Antro- bus's house. He went tothe house of the deceased, and saw alight in the kitchen, but there was no one in and he thought they must have gone somewhere else after returning. He did not fkl alarmed because he did not see them, and never thought of searching for them. By the foreman: The deceased were sober.—George Henry Bibby, letter carrier to the Weaver Trustees, deposed to seeing the bodies floating in the canal about seven o'clock. The bodies were about two yards from the ha.ndrailing of the bridgeover the entrance to the Salt Company's Dock.—P.C. Hamersley said he recovered the bodies. There were no marks of violence upon them and there was money in• the pockets. The•ciothing had not been interferred witibin any way. The old man with his left hand had hold of his wife's shawl at the neck, and his right hand was dirty and covered with cinders.—The Coroner :: That would lead one to believe that he had been trying toget her out. By the foreman: The bodies would be about four feet froim the handrail. —lnspector Bowyer: Anyone following the handrail as it is now would walk into the canal.—ln reply to the Coroner, Mr. Simister said the Bridge belonged to the Salt Company, and the towing path to the Ship Canal Company. His purpose in attending was to see if the jury made any recommendation.—The Coroner said any suggestions made to the Ship Canal Company with a view of saving life were always attended to. Reviewing the evidence the Coroner said the only conclusion the jury could come to was that these were two more deaths occurring through that terrible road from Weston Point to Runcorn, a road.which he had often described as a death trap, and it was nothing else but a deathtrap. He had made representations from time to time, in the hope that the authorities might be induced, by the loss of life which occurred on this road, to carry out a scheme, which they had nearly matured some time since, of making a direct road between the two places, but for some reason or other the road never seemed to he ad- vanced. So long as there was no road except along the towing path, so long should they have to hold these sad inquiries.—A juryman (Mr. Bloor) said this was the 82nd death in the canal since it was opened 28 years ago.— The forenlan asked if something could not be done to alter the rail.—Mr. Bloor said he was foreman for the Salt Company, and if the Ship Canal Company would give permission, he would extend the rail six or eseht feet on either side of the bridge.—Mr. Simister said he had no doubt the agent would at once communicate with the Salt Union if the jury made the recommendation.— The Coroner lam sure the jury make the recornmenda- tion.—The Coroner said he had gone to the trouble to ' search the records, and he found that since 1375, there had been 17 persons drowned in the canal, whose deaths might be directly attributed to that road, and upon whom inquests had been held at Weston Point. It was quite obvious that the road was more than ordinarily dangerous, for the deceased in this instance had lived at Weston Point for 23 years, and if anyone knew the road they did.—A verdict of "Found drowned" was re- corded.

div.head: HURRICANE IN THE UNITED STATES.
div.p: HURRICANE IN THE UNITED STATES.
LOSS OF OVER 500 LIVES.

Advices from New York, dated yesterday morning, say a terrific storm of wind, rain, and hailstorm is raging in the Western States, and many villages and towns have suffered greatly. The village of Little Prairie, in Illinois, has been completely destroyed, and hundreds of persons are reported to have been killed by falling roofs, trees, &c. Many other villages have also been partly wrecked by the extreme violence of the hurricane. Eye witnesses of the disaster estimate the ninater of persons killed in Louisville alone at two hundred, A large public hall, wherea dance was in progress', was levelled by the storm, and but few persons escaped from the mires, which almost immediately after the collapse caught fire.

div.head: FEINFIIEII DETAILS.
div.p: FEINFIIEII DETAILS.

The most recent reports only increase the magnitude of the disaster. In Louisville 2,500 buildings have been wrecked, and though it in yet impossible to accurately estimate the loss of life,, it if probable that more than 500 persons have perished. It is stated that dead lictiits are stacked about the city in heaps, whence the dis- tressed frirnds of the deceased are conveying the rernrins to their homes. The people are' beside themselves with grief and excitement. Seven d;stinct fires broke out almost simultaneously,occariened by the fall of materials upon domestic fire-places or by the overthrow of lamps land the like. The suburb= of Parkland is entirely des- troyed.

div.head: 11.ATEST• PARTICTTLARS.
div.p: 11.ATEST• PARTICTTLARS.

NEW Yon, FamAY.—Actording to latest estimate the loss of life by the tornado in the Louisville district will amount to nearly a' thousand. In the town of Metropolis, Illinois, 250' houses were destroyed, and several hundred people perished.
DEATH OF ki)T, OLD WARRINGTONIAN.

Warrington has. this week lost one of its oldest inhabitants, by the- death of Mr. William Davies, who was as highly esteemed: as he was well known amongst all classes of the community. In business he was a coppersmith, as wasliis father before him, and it is worthy of mention that the business has been carried on for seventy years in tile same premises-- 6, and 8, Lyme-st. Mr-Havies, Wag' born in the early part of the year 1814, and was, at thetime of his death in his 77th year. For some time befere his demise he had been in failing health 4 and,. although chronic bron- chitis is assigned as the immediate • cause. of death, fears had been entertained that his-constitutiorr was breaking' up by stress of years:. Personally,.. Davies was one of the most gentai of' men, and he was liked by a large circle of intimate friends, and a still larger circle of acquaintances: In politics, he was a Liberal, and a staunch one.. Comparatively early in life he embraced Liberal principles,., and his political, work dates from a period anterior to the passing of the first Reform Bill in 1832. He was a hard worker-at the elec- tion contest that resulted in the return of Mr. Peter Rylands for Warrington, and ithe tookan,active part in , the contest between Mr. Alldard and Sir (filbert Green- all. Notwithstanding his adriakted partiianship how- ever, he had the satisfaction of' numbering among his friends a few who were in polities opposed' to. him. One curious fact deserves mention. Mi. Davies' name and address has been the same on the voting list. since. 1832, a circumstance which perhaps could not be said of any other voter in the borough. The funeral took place at the cemetery on Thursday morning, the burial' service being conducted by the Rev; F2l‘. Fieeston. Many sympathising friends sent handsome wreaths:

The Parish Church of Guestling, near Hastings, was totally destroyed by fire on Sunday, through the ignition of the roof by means of a flue. The Church was very ancient, dating from the twelfth century, and contained various styles of architecture. A passenger train travelling on the old line of the Mid- land Company from Chesterfield to Sheffieldi via Mas- borough, on Wednesday night, ran into the rear portion of a goods ain, at South 'Junction, .Two .pesaen. gers—Mrs. Eastwood and Mrs. Vickers—were iqured.

THE KING OF THE BELGIANS.
The King of the Belgians visited Manchester on Thuri.. day, and on Friday inspected the Forth Bridge.
A BARQUE ASHORE.
The, Pforwegian barque Pasteur, of Arendal, from Mexico for Liverpool,laden with mahogany, went ashore in Carnarvon Bay. The crew were saved.

TWENTY THOUSAND ACRES AMERICAN PRO- PERTY FREE. In allotments of Farm, Fruit, and Vineyard Tracts of 40. 20.10, and 5 acres each, and selected Residence or Business Lots. ONE of the above divisions of Real Estate Pro- party, located either in the Golden State of fruitful California, or in the famous Orangegrove State of Florida, will be unconditionally given free from any charge for the land to any respectable person who sends his or her full name and post address to the American Office of the Californian and Southern Land Company at Cincinnati, Ohio, U.S.A. As soon as your name and address are received by the Com- pany, a free Land Warrant for one of the allotments of free property will be returned to you by first ocean post. The only cost for the property will be an expense fee for executing a Warranty Transfer Title Deed in your favour, and having the signatures thereto legally acknowledged before the pi oper officials. Such expense will in no case exceed 125., and is not to be paid until after you have received the Free Land War- rant. When one or more members of the same 'family, or , friends, wish to secure property together, the Company will issue to any applicant as many Free Land Warrants as may be requested, not to exceed ten, to be given by the applicant to those whom he applies for. The object in making this extraordinary offer is to secure a diversified interest and ownership throughout, the different countries of Europe in the lands owned and controlled by the above-notned Compa,ny. When this is accomplished, the Company will open branch offices in various European Cities, and offer its large remaining properties for sale at a uniform price of £5 per acre for Farm and Fruit Tracts, and £6 per Plot for Residence or Business Lots. It is believed by the Company that the diversified interest that will be thus secured by this preliminary method of advertising will amply compensate for the amount of pro- perty that is now offered FREE. If Liao number of names sent for free property is In excess of the amount of such property, those whose names are re- ceived first will secure it. Hence the advantage of sending name and address at once. All that need be sent is an envelope bearing your name and post address ; this envelope to be enclosed in another, and the outer envelope t,o'be addressed as follows: THE CALIFORNIA AND SOUTHERN LAND CO., CINCINNATI, OHIO. U.S.A. NOTE.--If preferred, application may be made to the Com- pany's Branch Office in London. A peony stamped self- addressed envelope sent to tke Company's London Agent, Mr. W. H. FULLER, 8, College Chambers. High Holborn. Lon- don, wiji secure a FREE LAND WARRANT, issued by the Home Company, the same as if lent direct to the Head Office.

LAnOUR AND CAPITAL. - At a conference of working men in Manchester, an Tuesday night, a resolution was unanimously adopted iri favour of the establishmeet of boards of conciliation for the adjustment of labour disputes. THE SWEATING COMMITTEE. In the House of Lords, on Monday, the Earl of DU raven formally announced his retirement from the chairmanship of the Sweating Committee by asking ta, be exempted from further attendance at the meetings ra: that body. His lordship did not make any statement of his reasons. ENGINEERS AND THEIR WAGES. A representative meeting of the masters of the varitala :1 I engineering establishments in Liverpool, and neighbourl hood, was held on Monday afternoon, when the demand ' of the engineers for an advance of 2s. per week in their wages was fully considered. It was resolved to concede the increase. „el, THE BERLIN CONFERENCE.—SOME IMPORT.a.O- - DECISIONS. The work of the Labour conference will not take more than a fortnight, and will probably come to an end neet -, Saturday. The "Berliner Politischer Nachrichten " declares that the labours of the Conference are already so far advaneed , that the final sitting may be expected on the 29th inst. The journal gives further particulars regarding the work . of the three Committees, which, it states, have alreadY arrived at the following important decisions :- 1. That only persons over fourteen years of age shall . I work in mines. 2. That female labour underground in mines is alto- gether inadmissible. ci- I 3. That children's labour in factories must be depen ent upon their having completed the authorized school course. 4. That night work for children under fourteen years of age is prohibited. 5. That in any case children under fourteen shall not work more than six hours a day, with an interval a 0 least a quarter of an hour. 6. That childreu's labour in unhealthy or dangeroue trades is forbidden. 7. That Sunday rest shall be conceded in all emplar ments, with the exception of certain cases in which Saa- day labour may be necessary for the continuity of the_ production or trade in which work can only proceed a; certain seasons of the year, and that even in these case the employe shall have at least every other'&unday free. THE POPE AND THE EMPEROR. The letters which have passed between the German Emperor and the Pope on the subject of the Labour Can- fereuce are published. His Holiness expresses wail° a be wishes for the success of the Conference, and saY_.,„a hopes that the servants of the Church will be supear''''; : by the authorities in the exercise of their functions a the 1 , social questiens. A correspondent at Berlin sacs it has been such unanimity in the Committees that ihe war , of the Conference is expected to terminate this week.

Her clothing was wet, and she was without the child. A search along the shore resulted in the discovery of the infant dead on the beach. The mother said she 'attempted to drown herself also, but the receding tide prevented her. She was taken beflre the Sheriff and remanded.
